items.model_answer:
If a carpenter from Nazareth—Jesus—had become King of the Jews in a political and historical sense, rather than being executed and later proclaimed a spiritual king by his followers, the trajectory of Jewish, Roman, and global history would likely have shifted dramatically.

First, his movement would have transformed from a marginal, apocalyptic reform movement into a political revolution within Judea. To become king, he would have needed either to defeat Roman authority or to gain recognition from it. If he had successfully led a revolt and established an independent Jewish kingdom, he might have fulfilled contemporary messianic expectations of a Davidic ruler restoring national sovereignty. In that case, his message would probably have emphasized law, governance, and national restoration more than suffering, humility, and spiritual salvation. Christianity, as it later developed around the theology of the crucifixion and resurrection, might never have emerged in the same form—or at all.

Alternatively, if Rome had installed him as a client king, his rule would likely have required compromise with imperial power. His teachings on loving enemies and rejecting violence would have faced tension with the realities of kingship—taxation, military enforcement, and political repression. The moral authority that later defined his legacy might have been diminished by the compromises of rule.

Most significantly, without crucifixion—the event that became the theological center of Christian belief—the interpretation of Jesus as a sacrificial savior may not have developed. The early Christian proclamation that his death and resurrection redeemed humanity was inseparable from his execution. A reigning king does not generate the same redemptive narrative as a crucified one. Christianity might have remained a Jewish reform sect tied to a particular kingdom, rather than evolving into a universal religion transcending ethnicity and empire.

In short, if the carpenter had become a political king, he might have changed Judean history in the short term—but it was his rejection as king and his death that enabled the rise of a global faith.

items.question: What If Princess Mary Tudor married Philip of Bavaria
human_answers: Wouldn't Philip Jr.'s surname be "Tudor-Palatinate"? While he was a male-line member of the House of Wittelsbach, Philip was the Duke of Palatinate-Neuburg (and his brother would become Elector Palatine after the death of their childless uncle) and Wittelsbach was mostly used for the Bavarian branch of the family, with the Palatine branches mostly using "Palatine-X" as their house name (like the Spanish Hapsburgs who used "of Austria" as their surname) Looking forward to see what will be Philip's religious education, although seeing as his father is Lutheran and his uncle would support protestant tutors he will probably be on the "low-key protestant" side of things. EDIT: Also will be interesting to see how the Palatine inheritance will work out on this TL, Philip the Contentious's older brother Otto-Henry became Elector Palatine in 1556 after their uncle, Frederick, died childless. And Otto-Henry would himself die childless in 1559 (he was married from 1529 to 1543, but no children were born, he was probably the one sterile since his wife had 11 children from a previous marriage). In OTL Philip died childless in the 1540s, meaning that the Electoral title passed to a cousin, but since in this TL he has children, I'm curious to see if there will be a personal union between England and the Palatinate or Mary will have a second son so they can divide the inheritance

For the last six years of her father's reign, Mary and Philip largely stayed out of court affairs, only returning for King Henry's last two marriages and Christmastide celebrations. While Mary's relationship with Kitty Howard was scarcely remarked upon before and after the unfortunate queen was executed, she and Catherine Parr had become close friends, with Catherine being godmother to Mary's third daughter, Mary just as Anna of Cleves was godmother to little Elizabeth. However, Mary's relationship with her father seemed to deteriorate as it was becoming quite clear that Henry was disappointed that he only had granddaughters. He even suggested that little Katherine should be raised in her aunt's household to make sure she didn't become as insolent as her namesake. Mary refused to speak to her father for a almost four months after that and it was only through Catherine Parr's intervention did Henry not go through with drawing up an act of succession that would skip over Mary and her daughters. When King Henry passed away in January 1547, Mary discovered she was pregnant again. Six months after her father's death, she gave birth to a son. She named him Philip after his father who greeted the birth of his son just as happily as he had the birth of his three daughters. There was some discussion over whether or not the boy would take his father's surname or his mother's as King Henry had decreed when Philip and Mary were first married. As his Uncle Edward's heir, some even wanted the boy to be raised somewhere else. Mary put her foot down, saying that if her husband's name was good enough for their daughters, it was good enough for her sons. She did not say a word about Phillip being taken from her. Of course, she hardly needed to as the Duke of Somerset, the Lady Elizabeth, Anna of Cleves and the Dowager Queen Catherine made it extremely clear to Edward, how utterly awful that would be. The boy-king himself wasn't too keen on the idea, considering he had never known his mother. In the end, Philip, Earl of Cambridge was known as Philip of Bedford and he would grow up in the Somerset household until he was six-years-old and started his formal schooling in Hatfield. Family tree: Philip, Duke of Somerset (b. 1503-) m. Mary of England (b. 1516). 1. Katherine of Somerset (b. 1540) 2. Elizabeth of Somerset (b. 1542). 3. Mary of Somerset (b. 1545). 4. Philip, Earl of Cambridge (b. 1547).
items.original_question: What if Princess Mary Tudor married Philip of Bavaria After a short courtship, King Henry announced that his daughter Lady Mary's engagement to Philip, Duke of Palatinate-Neuburg. Philip and Mary marry in early March in a small ceremony attended by the royal family and a few favored courtiers. Many expressed their displeasure at the match, chief among them the Imperial ambassador who wrote to the Holy Roman Emperor, lamenting that his poor cousin was now tied to a German Heathen who has no royal to speak of. The Earl of Hertford was similarly was not pleased with the marriage viewing any children Mary had as potential rivals to his nephew Prince Edward. Despite going through the process of getting a divorce from Anna of Cleves, King Henry remained on good terms with his son-in-law, even granting him the Duchy of Somerset once he abdicated his own duchy to his brother so he and Mary can stay in England. He was even happier to learn that Mary was pregnant with his first grandchild, requesting that the unborn son be named Henry for him. He was quite disappointed when on December 23, Mary had a daughter named Katherine instead.

If Princess Mary Tudor—Henry VIII’s sister and the former Queen of France—had married a Bavarian prince such as Philip of Bavaria instead of Charles Brandon, the political and religious trajectory of early 16th‑century England might have shifted in subtle but meaningful ways.

First, the immediate political impact would have been diplomatic rather than domestic. Mary’s historical marriage to Charles Brandon angered Henry VIII because it was made for love and without his formal approval, but it ultimately kept her within England’s political orbit. A marriage to a Bavarian prince would have strengthened England’s ties to the Holy Roman Empire, especially the Wittelsbach dynasty, which was deeply embedded in imperial politics. Depending on timing, this could have drawn England more firmly into Habsburg-aligned continental alliances, potentially tightening relations with Emperor Charles V.

Second, such a marriage might have influenced England’s position during the early Reformation. Bavaria was a staunchly Catholic territory and later became one of the strongest centers of the Counter-Reformation. If Mary had become integrated into that dynastic network, it could have reinforced conservative Catholic alliances around Henry VIII during the 1520s and 1530s. While it is unlikely that this alone would have prevented Henry’s break with Rome—since that was driven by his marital crisis and dynastic concerns—it might have complicated his diplomatic calculations. Stronger German Catholic ties could have made isolation from Rome more costly or politically delicate.

Third, the internal English consequences could have been significant in terms of succession politics. Mary’s historical marriage to Charles Brandon produced Frances Brandon, mother of Lady Jane Grey. That lineage played a central role in the succession crisis after Edward VI’s death in 1553. If Mary had married into Bavaria instead, Lady Jane Grey would never have existed, and the attempted Protestant coup placing her on the throne would not have occurred. In that case, Mary I (Henry VIII’s daughter) might have ascended the throne with less immediate resistance, potentially stabilizing her early reign.

Finally, Mary Tudor herself would likely have remained abroad, reducing her personal influence at the English court. Her marriage to Brandon kept her close to her brother and involved in court politics. A Bavarian marriage would have removed her as a domestic political actor and tied her fate more fully to continental dynastic struggles.

In sum, while Henry VIII’s break with Rome and the broader English Reformation probably still would have occurred, a marriage between Mary Tudor and Philip of Bavaria could have strengthened Catholic diplomatic alliances, altered succession politics by eliminating the Lady Jane Grey episode, and slightly reshaped England’s continental alignments during a pivotal era.

items.question: What If All of Anne Boleyn's pregnacies came to term
human_answers: When King Henry introduced the Oath of Supremacy he made it clear that it would be treason to refuse to sign it. Three Carthusian monks, a Bridgettine monk and priest had refused to sign it along with Thomas More and Bishop John Fisher. All of them now languished in the Tower awaiting their deaths. However six days before the monks and the priest were slated to die, Queen Anne dropped to her husband's feet and begged him to spare the seven godly men whose only crimes was being mislead by the Catholic Church. Had God not proved that she and Henry were just in their path by blessing them with Prince Ambrose. "I beseech you to pardon them my lord, spare them for they are ignorant not disloyal." Since the birth of Prince Ambrose, King Henry had been able to deny Anne anything. Although it infuriated him that his subjects were defying him, he had to admit that with the birth of his son, they had become a small number. So he officially pardoned all seven men, telling them it was only thanks to the Queen that they were alive, but not even she would save them if he caught a whiff of them trying to stir up trouble. Many wondered what had prompted Anne to ask her husband to spare these men, after all they were all her enemies and supporters of Katherine. Perhaps she had genuinely thought that now that she had a son, she had nothing to fear from those rabble rousers. Or perhaps she knew that the death of these men would only give Catholic more martyrs and that she would be blamed for their deaths. Meanwhile in Hatfield, Mary had fallen ill and Katherine sensing which way the wind was blowing wrote to Anne instead of Henry, imploring her not to think of her as her rival, but as a fellow mother who has been separated from her daughter and feared that her daughter might die. Anne wrote back that she would be delighted to reunite mother and daughter if Katherine would just acknowledge her as queen and her son as the Prince of Wales and her daughter as a Princess. She states that she does not need Katherine to admit to anything else, only to acknowledge her and her children. Katherine countered that she has been nothing, but a kind and goodly mistress to Anne so why did she insist on being so cruel and vindictive? Is it not enough that she had won? Must she continue to be so wicked? Anne sent another letter, asking Katherine what she would do if she was in Anne's position? Katherine noticeably did not answer and instead sent another plea, begging her to allow her to nurse her daughter back to health, swearing on her mother's grave that she will not say a single word against Henry, Anne, Elizabeth or Ambrose. Imploring her to take pity on an old woman who does not have much time left with her only living child. Anne could not refuse and she went to Henry, asking him to allow Katherine to visit her daughter. Henry did not refuse outright, instead he sent a letter to Katherine, admonishing her for putting poor pregnant Anne in the middle of their feud and telling her that Anne's insistence that she acknowledge Anne as Queen and Elizabeth and Ambrose as true heirs were far kinder than any demand he would have made for her. He told her point blank that she has two choices either sign the oath or do what Anne has asked of her. Katherine was fully aware that her daughter will never be accepted over a son especially with Henry's act of succession that allowed him to chose his heir. She also knew that despite his spiteful words after the birth of Prince Ambrose, her nephew wanted an English alliance and was reconsidering his stance. And as harsh as he was being, Henry was right. Anne's demand only required her to acknowledge Anne as Queen without denying the validity of her marriage or the legitimacy of her daughter or swearing that Henry was the head of the English Church. It was the lesser of two evils. Katherine finally agreed to acknowledge Anne as Henry's wife and their children as his heirs. She was allowed to leave Kimbolton Castle and reunite with Mary. While Mary was happy to see her mother, she was devastated to learn what her mother was going to do. Worse, Henry expected both Katherine and Mary to come to Whitehall and publicly acknowledge Anne as Queen. It was unknown what Katherine and Mary talked about as their watchers only reported that they did not speak treason. However, whatever her mother had said to her had evidentially convinced Mary that accepting Anne, Elizabeth and Ambrose was their only option. A week later, Katherine and Mary were welcomed at court where they had to sign a document declaring Anne Boleyn as the Queen of England, Elizabeth as a legitimate Princess and Ambrose as the Prince of Wales. It was unknown how their supporters took this news, but Anne's allies sighed in relief. As Thomas Boleyn continued to await his dukedom, he was pleased to learn that his son's wife is pregnant. In July, Anne Boleyn gave birth to a girl. King Henry decided that her name would be Anne after her most beloved mother.

So Anne has become more gracious in victory...or she is being pragmatic and has no wish to create more martyrs for the Catholic church than have already been made ( I figure that Thomas More has died already because his execution predates the PoD). Her actions toward Katherine of Aragon certainly suggest the former. Mary has agreed to drop her claims publicly, which probably cuts her deeply. At least she has her mother with her. And if she plays nice with an Anne who is gracious in victory (and Henry, who orchestrated her humiliations IOTL and ITTL), she might be restored to her father's good graces and get her legitimacy back (albeit after Anne's daughters and possibly Henry Fitzroy) and/or a marriage that isn't solely to undermine her claimed position in the suggestion. Speaking of Henry Fitzroy, how is he doing? I hope that he survives unlike OTL. Despite his words, Emperor Charles is recanting his position on the younger Tudors. I wonder if Philip/Elizabeth or Philip/Anne will happen ITTL?
items.original_question: What if All of Anne Boleyn's pregnacies came to term Despite popular belief, King Henry was not disappointed with the birth of Princess Elizabeth, believing if his wife could have a healthy girl, she could have a healthy boy. However, this did not change the simple fact that in order to to secure her position as Queen, Anne Boleyn desperately needed a son. Thankfully she did not need to worry for when she went into labor in August 26 and gave birth to a healthy boy. Anne Boleyn upon learning she had a son is said to have cried out: "If I die tomorrow, consider my blood well spent for I have done what I have promised and my son is my victory!" King Henry was over the moon. He had a son. It is said he wept for joy for at last England can rest easily now that there was a male heir. He claimed that his father must be smiling done from heaven, pleased that his dynasty was at least secure. Those who knew the late King Henry had a feeling that if the old monarch was indeed looking down at his son from heaven, he was not smiling. Regardless the birth of the new Prince was celebrated even by those who hated Anne Boleyn, blaming her for the King forsaking Katherine and Mary, it would take some time for the people of England to fully take her in their heart. Thankfully they wasted no time accepting her son as it had been over two decades since they celebrated a Prince of Wales. Thrilled with his wife, King Henry allowed her to chose the Prince's name, Anne wanting her son to have a name that no other monarch had before him, that would make him stand out in the mist of Thomases and Henrys chose to name him Ambrose, declaring that his legacy would be immortal. Her husband enthusiastically agreed even if he was disappointed that she had not named him Henry. It was said that the former Queen Katherine wept upon learning that Anne Boleyn had given birth to a boy. She sent a letter to congratulate Henry on having a son and begged him to allow her to see her daughter. King Henry wrote back he would be most pleased to do so if she and Mary would sign the oath and swear that Prince Ambrose is Henry's true heir. When Princess Elizabeth was brought to court, the Lady Mary was among her retinue. If she had hoped the invitation to court was a sign that her father was softening, that was dashed when King Henry refused to see her and instead sent a message that he expected her to be at her brother's christening for she would be his maid as well as her half-sister. Emperor Charles declares that the birth of a bastard "though he lorded as true prince of blood" changes nothing for his aunt is the true queen and his cousin is the true Princess of Wales. However King Francios, who was feeling quite discomforted by Lutherans thanks to the Affair of the Picards incident, is almost too happy to be godfather to young Ambrose along with his sister Marguerite. When he sends Philippe de Chabot, the admiral of France, in November, he is all to happy to agree to the betrothal of young Princess Elizabeth with his third son, Prince Charles. Queen Anne exited her time of confinement as though she was on cloud nine. She even invited her estranged sister to return to court for Christmastide, having convinced King Henry to knight William Stafford and make him a Baron. "There will be no getting rid of her now," Charles Brandon, Duke of Suffolk wrote to his wife. "She managed to convince His Majesty to send away his mistress. Now that she has a son, he is once again hanging off every word." Thomas Boleyn was ecstatic and fully expected to be made a Duke by next year. If all of Anne Boleyn’s pregnancies had come to term and produced healthy children, the course of English and possibly European history could have been significantly different. Historically, Anne gave birth to one surviving child, Elizabeth (future Elizabeth I), and suffered several miscarriages, including at least one widely believed to have been a male fetus. The central political problem of Henry VIII’s reign—his desperate need for a legitimate male heir—might have been resolved within his second marriage.

If Anne had borne Henry a healthy son soon after Elizabeth, her position at court would have been dramatically strengthened. Much of the hostility toward her stemmed from her failure to produce a male heir. A living prince would have secured the Tudor succession, reduced factional maneuvering, and likely prevented Anne’s execution in 1536. The charges against her—adultery, incest, and treason—were almost certainly politically motivated and tied to her failure to deliver a son. With a prince in the nursery, it would have been far more difficult for Thomas Cromwell and Anne’s enemies to engineer her downfall.

A surviving son by Anne would have displaced Mary (Henry’s daughter by Catherine of Aragon) further from the line of succession and reduced the later instability that followed Edward VI’s early death. If Anne had produced multiple surviving sons, England might not have faced the mid‑Tudor succession crises at all. Edward VI—Jane Seymour’s son—would never have been born if Anne had remained queen. Instead, Anne’s son would likely have succeeded Henry VIII directly. Depending on his health and longevity, there might have been no reigns of Mary I or Elizabeth I.

Religiously, the English Reformation may have taken a somewhat different path. Anne Boleyn was sympathetic to reformist ideas and patronized evangelical scholars. If she had remained queen for decades as the mother of the heir, reformist influence at court might have deepened earlier and perhaps more consistently. Mary I’s Catholic restoration (1553–1558) would likely never have occurred, meaning England might have avoided the Marian persecutions and the brief reconciliation with Rome. The Elizabethan Religious Settlement, as we know it, might also never have emerged, because Elizabeth herself might never have ruled.

Elizabeth I’s reign had enormous cultural and geopolitical consequences: the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the flourishing of English drama, and early overseas expansion. Without Elizabeth as queen, England’s foreign policy, relations with Spain and France, and early colonial ventures could have unfolded very differently. A son of Anne might have pursued a more aggressively Protestant alliance system—or, alternatively, sought continental marriages that reshaped European power balances in new ways.

In short, if Anne Boleyn’s pregnancies had all come to term, especially producing one or more healthy sons, her execution likely would not have occurred, Jane Seymour would not have become queen, and the later Tudor succession crises might have been avoided. The English Reformation would probably still have continued—since Henry had already broken with Rome—but its character, pace, and leadership would have differed substantially, and the iconic reign of Elizabeth I might never have happened.

items.question: What If Elizabeth Tudor marries Robert Dudley in 1550
human_answers: My son, You beg me for permission to marry that Rosbert girl and then you turn around and spurn her for the Lady Elizabeth. We shall be lucky if we don't lose our heads for this---please note that I said we---- I hear the Duke of Somerset is quite eager to make it happen. Don't fret boy, the King loves his sister too much to listen to his uncle and I think shall use that divide against the Lord Protector. You and the Lady Elizabeth will be invited back to court in a year's time, I am sure of it. If your blushing bride is reading this, I don't know how Robert tricked you into this, but I am most happy to welcome you into our family and I wish to reminded you that John is a very good name. Sincerely John Dudley, Earl of Warwick and Viscount of Lisle. Dear sweet cousin, Mother is in Heaven cheering. I have no doubt that Aunt Anne is happy too, after all she loved you very much and would want your happiness more than anything else. Francis is petitioning the King for us to come visit you. I hope he grants it for I must see you. From Catherine Knollys Brother, Let us go down the family tree, shall we? Father is both worried you will get your head chopped off and determined to use this to his advantage. Mother is fretting over how you must be fairing in such a "savage" country. Johnny is upset that you endangered yourself and our family by marrying a princess. Gilly and Harry are jealous that you got to marry aforementioned princess as you are not nearly as intelligent or handsome as they are. Their words, not mine. Mary and Kitty are too busy gushing about how romantic it is and how happy you and Elizabeth must be. As for me, I'm just hoping your luck will rub off on me. Cheers, Lord Ambrose Dudley. Sweet sister, I'm still angry at you, you know? I mean running off with Robert Dudley! What on Earth possessed you? It's not that I don't understand, Bess, you loved him even when we were children. I know I am four years younger than you, but not even I could miss the way you two look at each other. Nonetheless, you not only married completely beneath your station, you married without my permission, forcing me to take a strong position. Uncle wanted you to be thrown in the Tower but I said no and yet he continues to pester me. God, Father has left me to be surrounded with wolves. You are the only one I trust completely, Bess. That being said as much as it gladdens my heart that you would name your firstborn after me,I will not be angry if you choose a different name. Your loving brother and most forgiving King, Edward Tudor Rex.
items.original_question: What if Elizabeth Tudor marries Robert Dudley in 1550 A big scandal shook the Tudor court when it is discovered that the Lady Elizabeth has secretly married Sir Robert Dudley. Enraged by his sister marrying without his permission, Edward exiled both the Princess and her new husband to Ireland, swearing he will never speak to either again. To his credit, he lasted a week before he began to write to her. The Lord Protector Edward Seymour strongly suggested that the young couple should be arrested for this crime but even at his angriest, the boy King has no intention of punishing his favorite sister that harshly. He instead says if Elizabeth wished to act like her Boleyn aunt than she would be treated like her, sent away from court. "Better than to be treated like her mother," Ambrose Dudley quipped in a letter to his brother. Thomas Butler, the 10th Earl of Ormond comes to his cousin's rescue, giving her and her husband a comfortable estate to live in in Ireland. It is unknown what Mary Tudor thought of all this as she had her own problems with King Edward, concerning religion. She did however send her sister a curt congratulations on her nuptials. As for Elizabeth and Robert, instead of being upset at being in exile, they instead made the most of it by touring Ireland, getting to know the people and trying to see if they could settle any disputes between the Irish and the English. By the end of the year, Elizabeth was discovered to be pregnant with her first child. She wrote to her brother that if it is a boy she shall name him after her beloved brother and most forgiving king.

If Elizabeth Tudor had married Robert Dudley in 1550, the consequences would have been dramatic, but the scenario depends heavily on context. In 1550, Elizabeth was still Princess Elizabeth, her half-brother Edward VI was on the throne, and Dudley was the son of John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland, one of the most powerful men in England. A marriage at that point would have been a political alliance engineered by the Dudley family to secure influence over a potential future queen.

In the short term, it would likely have strengthened the Dudley faction at court. If Elizabeth later became queen in 1558 as she did historically, Dudley would already have been her husband and thus king consort. This would have eliminated years of speculation and courtship politics that characterized her reign. However, it would also have tied her legitimacy and authority much more closely to one noble faction, undermining her careful strategy of balancing competing interests.

The marriage would have faced serious political risks. When Mary I took the throne in 1553, Elizabeth was viewed with suspicion as a Protestant heir. If she had already been married to Dudley—whose family was deeply implicated in the failed attempt to put Lady Jane Grey on the throne—Elizabeth might have been seen as even more threatening. She could have been imprisoned longer, possibly executed, or permanently sidelined. The Dudley name was closely associated with the Jane Grey coup; being married into that family might have fatally damaged Elizabeth’s position under Mary.

If both survived Mary’s reign and Elizabeth became queen with Dudley as her husband, England’s foreign and domestic politics would have shifted significantly. Elizabeth’s historical strength lay partly in remaining unmarried, which allowed her to use marriage negotiations as diplomatic leverage with France and Spain. A prior marriage would have removed that flexibility. England might have been drawn more deeply into factional struggles centered on Dudley’s ambitions. His unpopularity among some nobles could have fueled rebellion, similar to later resistance against royal favorites in other reigns.

Religiously, the Protestant settlement Elizabeth enacted would likely still have occurred, as both she and Dudley were aligned with Protestant reform. But the regime might have appeared more partisan and less moderate, potentially intensifying Catholic resistance at home and hostility abroad.

In the long term, the biggest difference would depend on whether the marriage produced children. An heir from Elizabeth and Dudley would have prevented the eventual succession of James VI of Scotland in 1603. That would have delayed or prevented the Union of the Crowns, fundamentally altering the trajectory of British state formation.

In sum, an early marriage to Robert Dudley would probably have weakened Elizabeth’s political flexibility, endangered her survival during Mary I’s reign, and reshaped the succession. It might have produced a more factional, less stable Elizabethan monarchy—and possibly a very different future for England and Scotland.

edus.text: If Elizabeth Tudor had married Robert Dudley in 1550,
the consequences would have been dramatic,
but the scenario depends heavily on context.
In 1550, Elizabeth was still Princess Elizabeth,
her half-brother Edward VI was on the throne,
and Dudley was the son of John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland, one of the most powerful men in England.
A marriage at that point would have been a political alliance engineered by the Dudley family to secure influence over a potential future queen.
In the short term, it would likely have strengthened the Dudley faction at court.
If Elizabeth later became queen in 1558 as she did historically,
Dudley would already have been her husband and thus king consort.
This would have eliminated years of speculation and courtship politics that characterized her reign.
However, it would also have tied her legitimacy and authority much more closely to one noble faction,
undermining her careful strategy of balancing competing interests.
The marriage would have faced serious political risks.
When Mary I took the throne in 1553,
Elizabeth was viewed with suspicion as a Protestant heir.
If she had already been married to Dudley—
whose family was deeply implicated in the failed attempt to put Lady Jane Grey on the throne—
Elizabeth might have been seen as even more threatening.
She could have been imprisoned longer, possibly executed, or permanently sidelined.
The Dudley name was closely associated with the Jane Grey coup;
being married into that family might have fatally damaged Elizabeth’s position under Mary.
If both survived Mary’s reign and Elizabeth became queen with Dudley as her husband,
England’s foreign and domestic politics would have shifted significantly.
Elizabeth’s historical strength lay partly in remaining unmarried,
which allowed her to use marriage negotiations as diplomatic leverage with France and Spain.
A prior marriage would have removed that flexibility.
England might have been drawn more deeply into factional struggles centered on Dudley’s ambitions.
His unpopularity among some nobles could have fueled rebellion,
similar to later resistance against royal favorites in other reigns.
Religiously, the Protestant settlement Elizabeth enacted would likely still have occurred,
as both she and Dudley were aligned with Protestant reform.
But the regime might have appeared more partisan and less moderate,
potentially intensifying Catholic resistance at home and hostility abroad.
In the long term, the biggest difference would depend on whether the marriage produced children.
An heir from Elizabeth and Dudley would have prevented the eventual succession of James VI of Scotland in 1603.
That would have delayed or prevented the Union of the Crowns,
fundamentally altering the trajectory of British state formation.
In sum, an early marriage to Robert Dudley would probably have weakened Elizabeth’s political flexibility, endangered her survival during Mary I’s reign, and reshaped the succession.
It might have produced a more factional, less stable Elizabethan monarchy—
and possibly a very different future for England and Scotland.

items.question: What If Peter of Castile (Pedro the Cruel) marries an English princess in 1360s
human_answers: Oh that's very flattering. Thank you I think the TL you're proposing is plausible and interesting re: the development of ATL Castile and Caroline War. I'm not sure the marriage with Philippa of Clarence is the way to achieve it, though. I don't share others' concerns about her inheritance, but it doesn't necessarily fit into Edward III's plans to create spheres of influence for his sons. Philippa, if she's not marrying Mortimer (who had some smaller land claims in Ireland before inheriting the Burke estates through Philippa) would seem to make more sense for a Fitzgerald or Butler or a knight of the Garter who Edward wanted to establish as a peer without alienating anything from the crown. You could argue that I am overestimating the importance of these spheres of influence. (This is around the time that Lionel gets a Visconti bride -- an arrangement negotiated to put pressure on the papacy to approve the Langley-Flanders marriage, which demonstrates that Edward III still had an overarching and interconnected dynastic plan.) But this is a period in which the Black Prince set out his own foreign policy. He does not simply rubber-stamp his father's agreements. It is TBP's decision to end the Castilian alliance when Pedro executed the prisoners from Nájera. Just a few years later, TBP vetoed his father's alliance with Charles the Bad. All of which is to ask, how would it matter to the Black Prince that his niece is queen of Castile? Or would TBP end the alliance anyway if Pedro acts the way he did in OTL? Then there is also the issue of Pedro's not-great treatment of his wives. We don't know much about Lionel (relative to his four more famous brothers), but we see Edward III and Gaunt have very close relationships with their daughters. Edward made his favorite daughter one of the greatest landholders in England and Gaunt was so fond of his eldest daughter (apparently because she reminded him of his late first wife) that he didn't marry her off until her mid 20s. If Lionel has this sort of affection for Philippa then he may not be willing to entrust his daughter to a king like Pedro. (Though, honestly, I think this is a less important point. Not only only is it entirely speculative of Lionel's personal affections, but Lionel does demonstrate a commitment to his father's plans in going through with the Visconti match for the main purpose of furthering his brother's marriage prospects in Flanders. Still, I don't thin Pedro's treatment of his wives can be entirely discounted.) I very strongly suspect that the marriage contract handed the Ulster estate over to Lionel in its entirety and entailed it to his heirs, regardless of remarriage. Heiresses in weak negotiating positions often lost everything to their husbands and, considering both that a) Elizabeth de Burgh only became an heiress because her father was assassinated by his cousin -- i.e., the man who would inherit if Elizabeth did not -- and b) that Elizabeth's guardian was her mother, Maud of Lancaster, who was a member of the English royal family herself, it just seems very likely that the marriage contract gave Lionel everything. Maud was predisposed to favor the royal family as a relative herself and would be very strongly predisposed to screw over the Burghs who murdered her husband by disinheriting them in favor of Lionel.

To be fair, when the negotiations presumably happen (1366 or 1367 the latest) Philippa's father Lionel is alive, healthy and about to be married for the second time. I don’t think the perspective of Philippa inheriting his estates looks all that close at this point. Moreover, I don’t think that the perspective of Pedro potentially inheriting domains in England and Ireland should scare Edward all that much. If anything, they could potentially serve as a hook to ensure the favorable Castilian policy towards England or otherwise they can be easily confiscated (it’s not like Castile can really try retain those estates against the wishes of Plantagenets). If after Lionel dies Edward really wants to revert these estates back to the crown (although as mentioned before there are arguments for Edward not to do it), I think there is a really neat way to do it. Presumably Philippa’s dowry however large can it be (BTW how large can it be? Up to £10,000 perhaps?) would not be enough to pay for Black Prince’s army (even if ITTL Edward, helping the future husband of his niece, can be a bit more moderate in his pricing). While Pedro can raise some money on his own (he was ready to pay de Guesclin 200000 gold coins – presumably florins - in 1369, so he had some money, although of course it wouldn’t be enough to settle his OTL bill with Edward), he would probably still need to pledge some his territories in lieu of the rest of the payment. So, after Philippa inherits her father’s estates, the mortgage can be rearranged with English and Irish estates now serving as a collateral instead of Castilian territories. Or even perhaps these estates can be given to the Black Prince staight away in lieu of the rest of the debt. @material_boy , what do you think about the proposed PoD and some of its consequences? I have been toying with the victorious Pedro for several years now, but the perspective of modeling the alternative HYW always seemed to daunting. It was your amazing TL that inspired me to approach it. So your opinion would be especially appreciated (although of course I would be happy to hear feedback from everyone).
items.original_question: What if Peter of Castile (Pedro the Cruel) marries an English princess in 1360s UPD: I have updated both the PoD and who is the most likely bride for Pedro. See up-to-date details here and further ( link ). However all the potential consequences of Pedro surviving described in the second part of this message are still very much valid. UPD 2: Please find the TL draft for 1362-1364 in this message ( link ) I've always had a soft spot for Pedro the Cruel (aka Pedro the Just) of Castile. His victory over Henry of Trastamara would have monumental consequences both for Iberian Kingdoms and for Europe in general (I will list some of them further down). While there are a few threads on the forum discussing the possibility of his victory over Henry they are all rather short and usually either discuss earlier PoDs (e. g. Joan of England surviving and marrying Pedro) or more decisive battle of Najera (with Henry being killed or captured in battle). The former is definitely plausible, but would alter 1350s and 1360s quite a bit, while the later doesn’t strike me as all that consequential (after all in 1367 Henry has a son as well as two brothers who could potentially lead the Trastamara party to victory even without Henry). IMHO the main reason for Pedro losing the Castilian Civil War were not particular mistakes on his part or successful moves on Henry’s, but rather the military dominance of du Guesclin’s routier army over Castilian one. So, if we want Pedro to retain his throne, we need to either occupy or counterbalance routiers until the Caroline Phase of the Hundred Years’ War starts. The latter was successfully done IOTL with the help of Edward the Black Prince in 1367, but the relations between Pedro and Edward quickly deteriorated mainly because Edward didn’t receive his pay as per treaty of Libourne and thus Pedro was left to his own devices in 1368-1369 and was defeated and killed. Presumably Pedro didn’t pay Edward simply because he was unable to raise such an enormous sum. The PoD I present is Pedro marrying Philippa of Clarence as part of negotiations with English. Philippa is the eldest granddaughter of Edward III and has just reached marriageable age in 1367. IOTL, she married Edmund Mortimer but of course king of Castile is a way more prestigious match (there are conflicting records about when exactly Philippa was betrothed to Edmund IOTL, but for the purpose of this PoD let us pick the latest option 1368). Pedro on the other hand is in his thirties, has not legitimate issue and both his wife and his beloved mistress are dead since 1361. The purpose of the marriage is twofold: firstly, to bring Castile closer to England and secondly to be a neat way to subsidize Edward’s expedition. I am not sure how large Philippa’s dowry was IOTL, but presumably if she has a royal marriage, it definitely should be quite large. So Edward’s army can at least partly be subsidized with his niece’s dowry. I am not sure if such an arrangement is plausible, but if it does happen consequences are massive. Presumably if the relationship between the Black Prince and Pedro is unstrained (or at least is significantly better than IOTL), the second invasion of Henry and de Guesclin would seem futile and probably doesn’t happen. In 1369 the Caroline Phase begins (even if IOTL Charles V summoned Edward because he already realized that Castille would fall to Henry, which is debatable, ITTL Charles presumably understands that Edward would help Pedro no matter what and thus he might as well go on with his plan). Thus, Henry would have very little military support and will stand no chance against Pedro and his allies. Possible consequences of the PoD: 1. Castille itself has a radically different social structure. a. IOTL Henry and his heirs had to give out large parts of royal domain for their supporters from lesser nobility that formed new aristocratic elites (since pedristas were active until mid-1380s Trastamaras needed their continous support for an extended period of time and thus royal domain suffered greatly). Quoting from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: The new dynasty came to power having given lavish grants and titles to supporting nobles, and territorial concessions to their royal allies in France and the Crown of Aragon. Henry II’s initial hold on the crown was a tentative one. New men came to the fore demanding a share of the victory, and the king also granted them substantial privileges and lands. Historians have long argued that the first decades of Trastámara rule witnessed the disappearance of the old nobility, a nobility dating to the late eleventh and twelfth centuries, and its replacement by a new nobility. In reality, the transformation was signaled by the rise to prominence of lesser branches of the great old noble houses, with a few new lesser nobles rising to very high status. This promotion in rank was tied to the granting of large estates and to extensive royal privileges. Such erosion of the royal domain and authority had, in turn, disastrous consequences for Castile over the next hundred years. Not unlike France or England in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the rise of the nobility led to waves of violence and instability. Securely grounded in their new economic power and high standing, the Castilian nobility challenged royal authority and even coveted, as was the case in the reigns of John II and Henry IV, the control of the Crown. Pedro unlike Henry is a legitimate king and thus doesn’t need such drastic measures to obtain necessary support. b. In the first half of XIV century one of the main pillars of royal power was municipal nobility (or more precisely non-noble municipal knights). At first kings bought their support against magnates by granting municipal knights’ extensive privileges, but since the latter felt constant pressure by disenfranchised bourgeoisie, they continuously welcomed royal entrenchment in cities and thus by 1340s urban centers were under firm royal control. Once again, quote from Teofilo F. Ruiz-Spain's Centuries of Crisis 1300 - 1474: In less than 50 years the non-noble knights monopolized municipal offices in most Castilian cities, bought most of the land around the cities, and gained control, as they did in Burgos and Avila, of the most important ecclesiastical benefices. In return the king hoped for, and often received, their military support against the magnates and access to the cities’ fiscal resources. Moreover, as the non-noble knights gained control of their respective cities, they came into conflict with those below them. Pressured from below by the disfranchised petite bourgeoisie, the non-noble knights welcomed royal interference in the affairs of the cities and, by the 1340s, the takeover of municipal administration by royal officials (the regimiento) became a political reality. For a brief period, royal control of the urban centers became one of the most significant gains of the Castilian monarchy, but then the disorders of the late fourteenth century weakened royal control anew. IOTL many cities supported Pedro against Henry and thus were severely punished by victorious Trastamaras which greatly weakened both cities themselves and royal control over them. Thus, if Pedro retains his throne Castile is a lot more centralized with a strong royal power based on resources from a reasonably large royal domain as well as prosperous cities under firm royal control which is a stark contrast to magnate-dominated early Trastamara Spain. 2. Pedro IOTL had a firm alliance with Portugal. His uncle Pedro of Portugal helped him in his wars against both Peter of Aragon and Henry of Trastamara. When Pedro of Castile was slain, it was Portugal that was the main base for anti-Trastamara action in Iberia. Ferdinand of Portugal, Pedro of Castile’s cousin waged several wars against Trastamaras (first claiming the crown of Castile in his own right, later supporting John of Gaunt’s claim). Pedro of course is a very strong clamant to Portuguese throne in his own right, but he can further cement his claim by marrying Beatrice of Portugal to his son (who presumably should be born in early to mid 1370s roughly similarly to OTL Roger Mortimer birth date and thus ideally match Beatrice). Moreover, before Trastamara coup Portugal and Castile had the same allies and aligned economic interests (both benefited greatly from maritime trade between Northern Europe and Mediterranean, both had Genoa as a most important trade partner and England as a main ally outside of Iberia). IOTL when Portuguese interregnum happened the nobility was split with a significant portion of it supporting Trastamara claim. It were municipal elites of 4 main Portuguese cities (Lisbon, Porto, Coimba and Evora) that bankrolled anti-Trastamara faction. The main reason for these was economic (i. e. retention of profitable maritime trade with Genoa, England etc.) as well as desire to cancel Ferdinand’s pro-noble reforms (which were conducted in order to fund extremely expensive campaigns against Castille). If IOTL Pedro continues to rule Castille, Portuguese municipal elites have no reason to dislike the union with neighboring kingdom (because Ferdinan’s reforms would be unnecessary and Castile and Portugal economic and political interest would continue to be closely aligned) and thus we can encounter Castilian-Portugese union in 1380s. 3. Pedro had an advantage in the War of Two Peters against Peter of Aragon. Presumably if Henry of Trastamara is no longer a threat, he can continue pressing Aragon for economic, political (most important one being the termination of Trastamara support) and perhaps even territorial concessions (getting back Alicante, Elche and Orihuela as part of kingdom of Murcia) 4. If Pedro marries Philippa, presumably John Gaunt and Edmund Langley would have alternative brides. IOTL the marriages happened to establish a claim over kingdom of Castile. ITTL Pedro would have legitimate heirs related to English royal family without such a match and thus daughters of Peter with at best debatable legitimacy are not ideal brides for English prices. Does anybody have suggestions who John and Edmund would marry in such a scenario? 5. Perhaps the most consequential consequence of the PoD is alternative Caroline Phase of HYW. The battle of La Rochelle that crippled English fleet IOTL was won by Castilian navy. If Castile continues to be an English ally, Castilian navy either doesn’t participate or participates on English side. Thus, English are able to get significant reinforcements to Poitou and Saintonge as well as £12,000 that were supposed to be used to pay for service of local troops (IOTL this booty fell to the hands of Castilians). This potentially a least allows English to retain control over Poitou, Saintonge and Angoumois and perhaps even reverse some French gains made in previous years. Moreover with English fleet still dominating the waters around France, the main reason for the disastrous Great Chevauchee of 1373 is gone. ITTL, it makes a lot more sense to bring reinforcements by see, as was done in previous years. Thus, the Caroline Phase of HYW can be radically altered in 1372-1373, perhaps to the extent of it being a draw rather than decisive French victory. All these consequences seem rather juicy, but I am not sure if the marriage of Pedro and Philippa is all that plausible. What do you guys think? (of course if you have comments on consequences of PoD rather than the PoD itself, I would be happy to hear those too).

items.model_answer:
If Peter of Castile (Pedro I, “the Cruel”) had married an English princess in the 1360s, the political map of late medieval Western Europe could have shifted significantly, especially in the context of the Hundred Years’ War and the Castilian Civil War.

In reality, Peter was allied with England through Edward of Woodstock (the Black Prince), who supported him militarily against his half-brother Henry of Trastámara. However, Peter’s legitimacy was weakened by his controversial marriage to Blanche of Bourbon (whom he abandoned) and his turbulent personal life. A formal marriage to an English princess—perhaps a daughter of Edward III—would have transformed this loose military alliance into a durable dynastic partnership.

First, it would have strengthened Peter’s claim to the Castilian throne. An English royal marriage would have enhanced his legitimacy in the eyes of European courts and possibly deterred some internal nobles from backing Henry of Trastámara. It might also have secured more sustained English military and financial support. One of the main problems Peter faced was that, after the Black Prince’s costly campaign restored him in 1367, England’s support waned. A marriage alliance could have made Castile a strategic pillar of English policy rather than a temporary intervention.

Second, it would have had major implications for the Hundred Years’ War. Historically, after Henry of Trastámara seized the throne (as Henry II), Castile became a close ally of France. The powerful Castilian fleet helped the French defeat the English at sea, most notably at the Battle of La Rochelle (1372), which was disastrous for England. If Peter had remained on the throne with English backing—and especially if he were bound by marriage—Castile’s navy would likely have supported England instead. This could have shifted naval dominance in the Channel and Bay of Biscay, improving English supply lines to Gascony and possibly prolonging or strengthening England’s position in France during the later phases of the war.

Third, dynastically, such a marriage could have created Anglo-Castilian heirs with claims to both realms. While a full political union would have been unlikely, it might have produced long-term alignment between England and Castile, potentially affecting Iberian politics for generations. The Trastámara dynasty, which later ruled not only Castile but also Aragon and influenced the eventual unification of Spain, might never have come to power—or would have done so under very different circumstances. The later marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella, which united Castile and Aragon and sponsored Columbus, depended on the Trastámara line; a surviving Petrist dynasty tied to England could have altered the trajectory of Spanish state formation.

However, Peter’s own personality and governing style would still have posed problems. He alienated many Castilian nobles through harsh reprisals and centralizing tendencies. Even with English backing, internal rebellion might have continued, potentially drawing England into a prolonged and expensive Iberian conflict. If English resources were diverted heavily to Castile, this might have weakened their position in France instead of strengthening it.

In sum, an English marriage in the 1360s could have solidified Peter’s rule, prevented Castile’s alignment with France, and strengthened England’s maritime and diplomatic position in the Hundred Years’ War. The rise of the Trastámaras—and thus the later shape of Spanish unification—might have been delayed or transformed. Yet much would still have depended on Peter’s ability to reconcile his own nobility, something that even a powerful marriage alliance might not have guaranteed.

items.question: What If Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 Instead of 1492
human_answers: Lots of feedback and responses! Thank you all! I'll get to responding to other replies later on. The Crusades! That's a good point for the year 1092 and the 11th century. Also lots of good points here. Very good points. Crusader-style polities and principalities in the New World, given the attitudes of the 11th century. 1. Why wouldn't a less-weakened Muslim power establish their own colonies? As long as they're in Iberia or Morocco, they got a good chance of colonization with that geography, I think? 2. Also why not? What if the Apache or some other First Nations group taking over the North American interior, like a counterpart to the Mongols. Hopefully less bad and deadly and painful though, though that's probably too much to ask for when it comes to warfare in general. "What if the Americas were colonized by Europe beginning in 1292?" Could be worth it's own thread! Here in this one we're talking about what if 1092 instead of 1292, or OTL 1492.

That's a fun scenario to consider. One way to get Medieval America... Not sure about the naval tech of the time though. Or the ressources given the voyage between Europe and the Americas are going to be months long. These are the two crucial things that need to be fixed to get the possibility. The North Route via Greenland and Vinland probably is the best shot to make this work. Think the issue is the fact the Atlantic Ocean is pretty devoid of islands that can make effective island-hoping stops. There are the islands of Macaronesia (Azores, Canarias, Madeira, Cape Verde) close to Europe but otherwise it's a long trip until you reach the Carribeans or one of the American coasts. This isn't the same situation as the Pacific where you have tons of small islets... unless you go into ASB territory and raise the Azore plateau but that basically is making Atlantis a real thing... Naturally this situation limits the abilities of Muslim powers to colonize. Europeans at least have the Viking routes, even if that requires a successful Vinland. Though one has to remember the legend of Abu Bakr II of Mali, the most likely fictionnal predecessor of Mansa Musa. It's a stretch and we're more dealing with an African power than a European or Arabo-Muslim one, but the distance between West Africa and Brazil is a lot shorter... But then again, it's basing ourselves on a myth.

As for how would see a medieval colonization of the Americas, I would expect it happened across the Northern Atlantic and would likely focus first on the region around St Lawrence Bay, which offer several good settlements, than we would see it spread up the St, Lawrence River and later down the East Coast. Early settlements would simply be normal Norse settlements, and outside Norse settlers the main early source of “settlers” would be slaves. The need for labor would drive this slave trade and the victims of this slave trade would likely mainly come from the British islands, the Baltics, Central Europe and the post Frankish kingdoms in order of importance and it would likely disappear by the 13th century. The early settlements would likely mostly be peasants republics, as the Norse seems to mostly have established those on the frontiers. Over time we will likely see consolidation of power under large land owners both secular and ecclesia and the rise of city states. Also as the Norse runs into more powerful native societies, we may also see more centralized frontier states lead by Norse war leaders, these may also turn on the less centralized Norse states and begin to establish true kingdoms. As the population we also see the arrival of Low German merchants, who establish merchant quarters in the cities, we will likely see German artisans also moving. We could also see something like the Ashkenazi migration to Poland, but it’s more likely that Low Germans simply will fill that niche as they did in the Baltic and Nordic countries. This may result in the rise Low German city states. At the same time the Catholic Church will likely introduce more warm weather crops as the Norse moves south. As the economy of Norse America grows and expand, others will likely look into establish alternative trade route to it. Here we may see the Portuguese doing their own Columbus expedition in the early 15 century. At that point I would expect a European presence already in the Caribbean, even if it’s not fully developed. So the Portuguese establish trade routes to the Caribbean and introduce Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cash crops. We likely also see the rise off the African slave trade, but with greater European and Mestizo presence in the region already, it likely doesn’t reach OTL levels and the more traditional European structure likely means a more serfdom like structure for the African slaves. I suspect the Norse will run into the Mesoamericans in the 14th century and we will see it falling to Norse invaders or crusaders, with it being relative far away from Norse American strongholds (which will likely be the Mississippi and St. Lawrence basins and the East Coast), I expect the model of conquest will be more like the Baltic crusades. Conquest mostly by knightly monastic orders and Mexico under a knightly Grandmaster. We could easily see a repeat in the Andeans, but we could also just instead see Christian missionaries converting them.

I am not familiar with the shipbuilding industry, but I believe this is possible. There was no fundamental difference like scale or materials between shipbuilding in the 15th and 11th century. They likely needed only to devise a few new designs, or simply undertake bold try using the vessels they already have. As for the difference? An 11th-century conquest of the Americas would have been far more likely to result merely in the emergence of independent states, rather than colonies subservient to Old World powers. At best, the Italian city-states might have established a few small commercial colonies (perhaps in the Caribbean region?), but inland colonies dominating an entire continent would have been highly unlikely. This aligns more closely with the norms of that era, and the comparatively weaker commercial and artisanal capabilities of Europe would not have generated the centripetal force required to establish such a relationship; Europe could not produce so many goods that American colonists were unable to manufacture for themselves. Two rather interesting questions: 1. Could a less weakened Iberian/North African Muslim power have established its own colonies in the Americas? 2. Could a nomadic polity have been established in the North American interior?

The major issue is that open ocean travel isn't really possible before the 15th century so you'd be island hopping like the Norse did. That's certainly possible but your probably looking at a more Polynesian or Greek heroic age style model (or for that matter the Norse in Iceland and Greenland) where people are leaving to found a separate colony rather than one controlled from the Metro-pole as its to far away. Also most of the early arrivals will be in the North (Canada, then moving into New England and points south as the Little Ice age bites) and while trade webs will probably see the European diseases spread there is a good chance the native powers will have time to recover before actual Europeans reach them. That could allow the Mexican civilizations and the Inca a good chance to survive especially if they've obtained European tech in trade before the newcomers have the forces to go after them (the Aztec are probably doomed whatever as the events of OTL strongly suggest they were hated by all and someone was taking them out eventually). Also its likely they understand pretty quickly this is a new land and not a route to China (or at least not an easy one, especially once they finally sight the great desert of the Plains prairie and realize just how big America really is) so there will probably be a much stronger focus on going south to round Africa to reach the Spice islands. With actual transoceanic travel developed much earlier (and the need to improve links with the New World driving sailing tech along at a fair clip) that's likely to see Portugal starting its investigations long before Spain is finished with the Reconquista and probably with England and France nipping at her heels this time. An early rediscovery (or more dissemination of the original Norse discovery) probably doesn't completely prevent the Crusades (there is still the issue of Jerusalem) but with a bigger target for expansion and as an outlet for violence the majority of settlers will probably go there rather than the rather precarious Outremer and even if the First Crusade succeeds it may not establish an enduring polity (they had enough trouble getting immigrants as it was. Usually Europeans only went East when the states were in deep trouble). Although with a Europe that has an outlet for its expansionist desires in the Far West and doesn't feel so under siege for the first time in centuries might be able to patch things up with Islam a bit more easily. Hard to say about Religion although by 1092 the Great Schism has already happened so the Catholics will be very much the first ones there and its hard to say if there will even be a Reformation after four centuries of altered history. However if the Crusades are averted, or at least blunted there is a good chance Byzantium survives in its original form and without the damage from the Latin occupation it might be able to hold out and reform enough that they can avoid falling to the Ottoman's. Also Venice and the Italian city states may not rise as quickly if the focus on trade switches to the Atlantic (especially if the wealth of America is discovered).
items.original_question: What if Europe colonized the Americas four centuries earlier? 1092 instead of 1492 What if widespread European colonization of the Americas started 400 years earlier in 1092, the end of the 11th century? The idea I got in my head so far involves rapid advances in naval/seafaring technology to allow for trans-oceanic voyages, and the sponsor of the first voyage and colony I'm thinking would be the Duchy of Normandy, but this can change if that's not plausible enough. What I want out of the timeline spawned by the question of thread title, is a medieval retro-future colonial-frontier sort of scenario, also going by another idea-spawning question. What if the 11th century had the technology of the 15th century? What sort of tech advances, and other sorts of points of divergence, would be needed to make the beginning of European colonization of the Americans begin its proliferation in 1092 instead of 1492? And what other ideas and questions and things should I also take into consideration? My apologies for not being able to go in-depth at explaining scenarios. I'm unfortunately a very simple person with a limited education and understanding of history and other topics needed for writing alternate history. I hope to get a discussion going that will help broaden my horizons of learning more history to write better alternate history.

items.model_answer:
If sustained European colonization of the Americas had begun around 1092 instead of 1492, the trajectory of global history would have shifted dramatically—but not simply by moving the familiar Age of Exploration four centuries earlier. Medieval Europe was politically fragmented, technologically more limited, and economically less dynamic than Renaissance Europe, so the nature, pace, and consequences of colonization would likely have been very different.

First, the feasibility of sustained colonization in 1092 is uncertain. European maritime technology at the end of the 11th century was far less advanced than in the late 15th. Navigational tools like the magnetic compass were only beginning to spread in Europe, and Atlantic sailing techniques were underdeveloped outside Norse experience. The Vikings did reach North America around 1000, but they failed to establish lasting colonies partly because European states lacked the naval capacity, population surplus, and centralized financing to support transatlantic ventures. For colonization in 1092 to succeed, Europe would have needed either stronger maritime states earlier—perhaps in Scandinavia or the Iberian Peninsula—or sustained institutional backing from powerful monarchies or the Church.

If such backing had existed, colonization would likely have been slower, smaller in scale, and more decentralized. Medieval Europe had a much smaller population than in 1492, and its economy was less commercialized. Colonies might have resembled frontier outposts or crusader states rather than massive extractive empires. Feudal structures could have been transplanted across the Atlantic, producing semi-autonomous lordships owing allegiance to distant monarchs. The Church would likely have played a dominant role, framing expansion as a missionary enterprise akin to the Crusades.

The most transformative consequence would still have been epidemiological. Even in 1092, Europeans carried Old World diseases such as smallpox, measles, and influenza. Indigenous American populations, lacking immunity, would likely have suffered catastrophic declines, just as they did after 1492. However, because medieval Europe had a smaller population and less intense commercial integration, the demographic collapse in the Americas might have unfolded more gradually. Ironically, Europe itself would soon face the Black Death in the mid-14th century. Earlier American contact could have altered disease patterns in both directions, though it is uncertain whether major American pathogens would have significantly affected Eurasia.

Economically, Europe in 1092 was not yet positioned to exploit American silver and agricultural wealth on a massive scale. The price revolution of the 16th century, fueled by New World silver, might instead have occurred in the 12th or 13th century, potentially accelerating the decline of feudalism and the rise of monetary economies earlier. Alternatively, limited extraction capacity might have meant that American resources had a muted global impact. Crucially, earlier access to American crops—maize, potatoes, tomatoes—could have boosted European agricultural productivity centuries sooner, possibly mitigating famines and reshaping medieval demography. A more populous Europe before the Black Death might have experienced either a worse pandemic shock or a different recovery trajectory.

Global power balances would also shift. If Iberian kingdoms or Scandinavian powers had established early American footholds, they might have risen to dominance earlier. The Islamic world, then economically and scientifically more advanced than much of Europe, might have responded competitively, possibly expanding westward across the Atlantic if knowledge spread. China’s Song dynasty, technologically sophisticated and maritime-capable, might have entered transoceanic competition if aware of American lands. In this scenario, the Americas could have become a contested multipolar frontier rather than predominantly European-controlled.

Most profoundly, Indigenous American civilizations such as the Aztec and Inca empires would not have existed in their later 15th-century forms. Four centuries earlier, political configurations in Mesoamerica and the Andes were different. Earlier contact could have interrupted the rise of large centralized empires, producing entirely different patterns of alliance, resistance, and cultural exchange. Some societies might have integrated European technologies gradually rather than facing sudden conquest by gunpowder states.

In sum, colonization beginning in 1092 would likely have been slower, more feudal, and less globally transformative at first—but over time, it could have accelerated Europe’s economic and political development centuries earlier. The Columbian Exchange would still have reshaped the world, but within a medieval framework rather than a Renaissance-capitalist one. The result might have been an earlier rise of Atlantic-centered power, a restructured medieval world economy, and profoundly altered paths for both European and American civilizations.

items.question: What If Henry dies in the joust and Anne gives birth to a son
human_answers: Judgement Day had finally come for Anne Boleyn. Allies and enemies, alike held their breath when the news broke that King Henry's widow was giving birth. It had been a miracle that she had managed to not miscarry on that fateful January day when her husband had fallen from his horse and would never wake up. When she had learned of Henry's death, Anne had fallen to her knees crying hysterically. However once her tears have passed and she has been calmed down, she immediately summoned the lords to form a regency council, making it clear that she will be regent, a fact that does not sit well with her uncle. Princess Elizabeth would be brought to court, both as a comfort to her mother, and in case she needed to be crowned. Lady Mary was removed from Hatfield and instead put under close guard at Hudson. The Seymours were sent away in disgrace. It was said that Queen Anne took a special delight in dismissing Jane Seymour, mocking her for ever thinking she could replace her. All of Europe held their breath as they waited to see what would happen. Not even the Pope was willing to make a move just yet, wanting to see where the land would lay. Finally on May 19, Anne went into labor. After ten grueling hours, the queen dowager finally brought her second child into the world. "Tis a healthy boy, Majesty, you have done it! You have birthed a prince!" the midwife exclaimed. "Nay, not a prince. A King. I have birthed a King!" Anne cried, a radiant smile on her face. "King Henry the Ninth!"
items.original_question: What if Henry dies in the joust and Anne gives birth to a son Might make this a full TL. Not sure yet. Here is what I am wondering. Let's say that Henry dies and Anne carries her son to term. What happens? Would the people pick Mary when there is chance for a male heir? I know Norfolk and his ilk would probably not turn on Anne when there is a chance that he could be Lord Protector for fifteen years. What about Elizabeth in the meantime, would she be crowned before Anne gives birth just in case Anne gives her a sister?

items.model_answer:
If Henry VIII had died from his jousting accident in January 1536 and Anne Boleyn had subsequently given birth to a healthy son, the immediate result would have been a male Tudor heir—an infant king (effectively Henry IX)—with Anne as queen mother and central figure in the regency government.

Because the boy would have been born to a reigning king and crowned almost immediately after birth, his legitimacy under the 1534 Act of Succession (which recognized Anne’s marriage and invalidated Mary) would have been difficult to challenge legally inside England. However, his position would not have been uncontested. Mary, Henry’s daughter by Catherine of Aragon, still had strong support among conservatives and those loyal to Rome, and Emperor Charles V (her cousin) might have backed her claim diplomatically or even militarily. England could have faced serious factional tension, possibly even rebellion, centered on Mary’s cause.

Domestically, Anne would likely have headed a regency council dominated by reformist figures such as Thomas Cromwell and Thomas Cranmer. Without Henry’s later conservatism and erratic interventions, the English Reformation might have advanced more consistently in a Protestant direction during the 1530s and 1540s. The dissolution of the monasteries would almost certainly have continued, both for ideological and financial reasons. The Church of England might have adopted more explicitly reformist doctrines earlier than it did under Edward VI.

Anne herself would not have fallen in 1536, since the political crisis that destroyed her was tied to her failure to produce a living son and Henry’s desire to remarry. As queen mother to a male heir, her position would have been far stronger, though still vulnerable to factional intrigue. Her survival would also mean no marriage to Jane Seymour and no separate reign of Edward VI; the Protestant succession would be secured through Anne’s son instead.

In the long term, this scenario likely prevents the reigns of both Mary I and Elizabeth I as we know them. Mary’s path to the throne would be blocked by a legitimate male heir, and Elizabeth would remain a secondary princess unless her brother died young. If Anne’s son survived to adulthood, England would probably remain firmly Protestant without the sharp Catholic restoration under Mary or the distinctive Elizabethan religious settlement. The mid-Tudor instability of the 1540s and 1550s might have been reduced—but only if the regency weathered the dangerous early years without civil conflict over the succession.

nodes.text: If Henry VIII had died from his jousting accident in January 1536 and Anne Boleyn had subsequently given birth to a healthy son,
the immediate result would have been a male Tudor heir—an infant king (effectively Henry IX)—with Anne as queen mother and central figure in the regency government.
Because the boy would have been born to a reigning king and crowned almost immediately after birth,
his legitimacy under the 1534 Act of Succession (which recognized Anne’s marriage and invalidated Mary) would have been difficult to challenge legally inside England.
However, his position would not have been uncontested.
Mary, Henry’s daughter by Catherine of Aragon, still had strong support among conservatives and those loyal to Rome,
and Emperor Charles V (her cousin) might have backed her claim diplomatically or even militarily.
England could have faced serious factional tension,
possibly even rebellion, centered on Mary’s cause.
Domestically, Anne would likely have headed a regency council dominated by reformist figures such as Thomas Cromwell and Thomas Cranmer.
Without Henry’s later conservatism and erratic interventions,
the English Reformation might have advanced more consistently in a Protestant direction during the 1530s and 1540s.
The dissolution of the monasteries would almost certainly have continued,
both for ideological and financial reasons.
The Church of England might have adopted more explicitly reformist doctrines earlier than it did under Edward VI.
Anne herself would not have fallen in 1536,
since the political crisis that destroyed her was tied to her failure to produce a living son and Henry’s desire to remarry.
As queen mother to a male heir, her position would have been far stronger,
though still vulnerable to factional intrigue.
Her survival would also mean no marriage to Jane Seymour
and no separate reign of Edward VI;
the Protestant succession would be secured through Anne’s son instead.
In the long term, this scenario likely prevents the reigns of both Mary I and Elizabeth I as we know them.
Mary’s path to the throne would be blocked by a legitimate male heir,
and Elizabeth would remain a secondary princess unless her brother died young.
If Anne’s son survived to adulthood,
England would probably remain firmly Protestant
without the sharp Catholic restoration under Mary or the distinctive Elizabethan religious settlement.
The mid-Tudor instability of the 1540s and 1550s might have been reduced
but only if the regency weathered the dangerous early years without civil conflict over the succession.
