items.model_answer:
In a world where the European Axis won, 2001 would not look like a static continuation of the 1940s, but like a technologically modern, politically rigid, and culturally stratified authoritarian order shaped by decades of fascist dominance.

Europe would likely be organized into a German-centered continental empire. Western Europe might exist as formally sovereign but subordinated states integrated into a German-led economic and military bloc. Eastern Europe would probably have been radically transformed: borders redrawn, populations displaced or forcibly assimilated, with large areas settled or administered directly by German authorities or their collaborators. Russia, if it still existed as a state, would likely be fractured, reduced to a rump regime east of the Urals, or permanently weakened after territorial partition.

The Holocaust and other genocidal campaigns would have permanently reshaped the continent’s demographic structure. Jewish communities in Europe would be nearly eradicated. Roma, Slavic populations in certain regions, and political dissidents would have faced systematic repression for decades. By 2001, overt mass killing might no longer be central state policy, but racial hierarchy would remain embedded in law, education, and citizenship. The regime might present itself as having “stabilized” and “civilized” its empire after an earlier brutal consolidation phase.

Technologically, 2001 would still be advanced. Industrial modernity, computing, aerospace research, and perhaps even space exploration would have developed, especially if rivalry persisted between a German-dominated Europe and another great power such as the United States or Imperial Japan. If the U.S. remained independent, the 20th century might have been defined by a long cold war between a democratic Atlantic bloc and a fascist Eurasian one. In that case, 2001 could resemble a high-tech surveillance civilization, where aerospace achievements and consumer electronics coexist with intense internal security systems.

If instead the Axis achieved overwhelming global dominance, technological progress might have been uneven. Innovation would likely concentrate in military, surveillance, and prestige projects, while intellectual life would be tightly controlled. Universities would operate under ideological supervision. Scientific inquiry conflicting with regime dogma might be suppressed, though pragmatic authoritarian regimes often tolerate science that strengthens state power.

Culturally, public life would be saturated with symbolism: monumental architecture in capital cities, mass rallies (possibly transformed into televised spectacles), and a media environment designed to reinforce unity and hierarchy. Television and the internet, if developed, would be filtered through state-controlled networks. By 2001, censorship might be technologically sophisticated rather than blunt—algorithmic filtering rather than book burnings.

Social mobility would depend on racial classification, party loyalty, and service to the state. Elite institutions would groom a transnational ruling class loyal to the imperial center. Everyday life for many people might appear superficially normal—jobs, schools, entertainment—but bounded by political conformity and limited civil liberties. Dissent would exist, but underground or in exile.

Globally, decolonization would likely have taken a different path. If European empires were reinforced rather than dismantled, Africa and parts of Asia might remain under direct or proxy colonial administration well into the late 20th century. Alternatively, anti-colonial insurgencies might have produced decades of insurgent warfare against Axis-aligned regimes.

In short, 2001 in a world where the European Axis won would probably be modern but unfree: technologically sophisticated, geopolitically rigid, demographically scarred, and organized around a durable hierarchy of race, nation, and party. It would not be frozen in 1945 aesthetics, but it would carry the institutional and moral architecture of a fascist victory into the digital age.

items.question: What If Israel existed during the Holocaust?
human_answers: Chapter 1: Independence In Geneva, the League of Nations debated the partition of Palestine for three days. While the world deliberated on whether there would be a Jewish state, the Jewish leaders engaged in a battle over whether to accept one, should it be offered. Dan, who had accompanied Ben-Gurion to Geneva, found it unconscionable that some of his people’s leaders could be against partition when the Jews in Germany were suffering such persecution. The Old Man faced constant anger from those who believed the Zionist Movement should refuse any deal that gave the Jews less than the entirety of the Land of Israel. These were the same people who had opposed Ben Gurion’s transfer agreement with the Nazis in 1933, even though it had allowed Dan to bring new emigrants to Palestine. Rabbi Stephen Wise, a leader of the American Reform Movement, had been pushing for a boycott of Nazi Germany for years and continued to decry the ongoing dealings with Berlin. He buttonholed Ben-Gurion in the lobby of their hotel as Dan accompanied his boss to the Palais des Nations for the final vote on statehood. “I can only express revulsion at your attitude,” the rabbi said. Fifty thousand people—fifty thousand—packed Madison Square Garden at a rally in support of a total boycott of German goods not long ago. Macy’s, Gimbel’s, Sears & Roebuck, Woolworths, and a good many other major American stores have removed German goods from their shelves and ended all commercial transactions with Germany. How can our people in Palestine, to whom we all turn for moral leadership, do anything less?Dealings with the Nazis of any sort are abhorrent, but your signed agreement is despicable. Now you would do a similar deal with the entire world, in which you will agree to sign away our Jewish birthright in favor of a mini-state just so you can have control over it.” Ben-Gurion rubbed his belly as though Wise’s attack disturbed his digestion. “The calamity that has befallen the Jews of Germany casts a shadow over all else. Trading with Hitler is acutely distasteful, but if that’s what is necessary to save Jews and bring them to Palestine, I will deal with the Nazis—even if it brings benefit to them. It is a true Zionist answer to Nazism. ”To Dan’s eye, Wise looked remarkably like the White Anglo-Saxon Protestants who ran Harvard. The rabbi was tall, with a thin mustache and a long, aristocratic face set in a combative frown even when he wasn’t angry. But now he was angry. “You’re dealing with the devil.” “How else are we going to save Jews? How do you get an agreement unless the other side—in this case, the Nazis—sees something to its advantage in it?” “It pains me to say this, but your whole attitude is dishonorable. You are behaving like a Levantine merchant at the expense of the honor of the Jewish people.” Dan caught his breath. “Levantine” was, after all, a euphemism for the grasping, untrustworthy Jew of anti-Semitic prejudice. But the Old Man was a master of the unfair rhetorical advantage, easily able to shame a critic for his anger and shut him down.“ Rabbi Wise, we are old colleagues, so I shall ignore your impetuous comments. Just let me say that the difference between us is that I have to deal with harsh Jewish realities, not virtuous American liberalities. While you, American Zionists, are mounting your boycott campaigns, we Jews in Palestine are struggling to provide a safe haven for German Jewish refugees—refugees to whom your president is denying entry to the United States. We have to find a practical Zionist response. Speeches in Madison Square Garden do nothing.” The rabbi took a step back, as though Ben-Gurion had jabbed his chin. He turned and went quickly from the hotel. Ben-Gurion twitched his head to the side. “You think I made a mistake, Dan?” “He’s quite an influential man.” “American Jews will support us once we have a state. So will Rabbi Wise.” “If we lose the vote today, there’ll be nothing for them to support.” “If we lose today, there’ll be nowhere for Germany’s Jews to go. That’s what I care about. Come on.” They walked to the Palais, where Ben Gurion tapped every last influential contact he could find outside the hall. At the end of another day of arduous debate, amid a hush blotted by nervous coughs, the representative of each state responded to the question of partition in Palestine with “Yes,” “No,” or “ Abstention.” When the last country’s vote was heard, the Assembly Hall erupted. The Resolution was accepted. Palestine was divided. The Jews had a state. Ben-Gurion fought his way out of the chamber through a scrum of exhilarated well-wishers, shepherded by Dan Lavi. Neither spoke as they crossed the Avenue de la Paix to their hotel. Ben-Gurion stomped along with his eyes to the ground, as though he were making his way through a repulsive slum in the dead of night, but Dan took in everything around him with the kind of joy that comes to a man who has just seen the luminous face of his child for the first time. The Alps shone in the spring sunshine, and the breeze off Lake Geneva seemed to carry him with it like a dancing partner. The phone rang as they entered their suite. Dan ran to pick it up. Through earsplitting static as raucous as the atmosphere in the Assembly Hall had been, the international exchange connected him to Jerusalem.“ Can you hear me?” Shmulik shouted. “Is the Old Man with you?” “Yes. I’ll give you to him now. Isn’t it a miracle, Shmulik? A state for us. For the Jews.” “We’ll need another miracle to keep it. Give me the Old Man now.” Ben-Gurion grabbed the phone, growling impatiently. He listened as his intelligence adviser spoke. Finally, he demanded to know, “What’s that din I hear in the background? Celebrations? Are they meshuga?” He hammered the phone down. Dan caught the heaviness in his boss’s demeanor. The struggle wasn’t finished. It was barely beginning.“Shmulik reports that the Arab armies are already on the move.” Ben Gurion slumped into a wing chair, but was uncomfortable in its stiff leather and upright back. He stood and punched a hand down on the side of the chair. “We have the independence we wanted. Now we are to have our war to keep it." (This is an excerpt from the book "The Ambassador" by Yehuda Avner. I wanted to see what you guys think of this type of narrative style-presentation. The rest will be from me after this.)

items.original_question: What if Israel existed during the Holocaust? This idea, inspired by the book "The Ambassador", will focus on an alternate reality where the Peel Commission is accepted by the British in 1937, in the same way as the UN partition plan was received in 1947. "You will sup with the Devil. You will do everything the Devil requires. Whatever it takes, you will maintain the transfer of Jews from Germany to Israel. Remember not to fear him. After all, he thinks it is you who the Devil is." -David Ben Gurion, to the future Ambassador to Nazi Germany, 1938.

If a sovereign, militarily capable State of Israel had existed during the Holocaust (roughly 1933–1945), several major dynamics of European Jewish history—and possibly aspects of World War II—might have unfolded differently. However, the extent of change would depend heavily on Israel’s political strength, military capacity, immigration policies, and relationships with other powers.

First, the most immediate impact would likely have been as a refuge. One of the central tragedies of the Holocaust was that millions of Jews were trapped in countries that either persecuted them or refused them entry. If Israel had existed as an independent state with control over its own immigration policies, it could have accepted large numbers of Jewish refugees. This would have required logistical capacity—transport routes, funding, housing, and agricultural or industrial infrastructure—but even partial success could have saved hundreds of thousands or potentially millions of lives, especially in the 1930s before World War II fully erupted.

Second, Israel’s diplomatic and military posture would have mattered greatly. If it had been a recognized sovereign state aligned with Britain or the Allies, it might have lobbied more aggressively for international action, conducted rescue operations, or even engaged militarily against Nazi forces in certain theaters. However, its geographic location in the eastern Mediterranean would have placed it in a vulnerable position, especially if Axis powers sought to expand influence through North Africa or the Middle East. In fact, during the real war, Nazi Germany did attempt to advance through North Africa; a Jewish state in the region could have become a strategic target.

Third, the existence of Israel might have altered Zionist migration patterns before the war. Historically, Jewish immigration to British-controlled Palestine was restricted during crucial years. An independent Israel could have removed those quotas. This might have significantly reduced the Jewish population remaining in Eastern and Central Europe by the late 1930s, thereby reducing the number of Jews ultimately exposed to Nazi extermination policies.

However, it is unlikely that Israel’s existence alone would have stopped the Holocaust within Europe. Nazi antisemitism was ideological and genocidal; the regime’s goal was not simply to expel Jews but to eliminate them. Jews who remained in Nazi-controlled territory would still have faced persecution and mass murder. Moreover, wartime blockades, transportation barriers, and the speed of German conquests would have limited evacuation efforts after 1939.

There is also the possibility that Nazi propaganda might have exploited the existence of a Jewish state to intensify antisemitic narratives within Europe, claiming Jews had a foreign national loyalty. Whether this would have materially changed policy is uncertain, since Nazi ideology was already extreme and exterminationist.

In sum, an existing State of Israel during the Holocaust would most plausibly have saved significant numbers of Jews by providing refuge and political advocacy, particularly in the 1930s. It may also have played a military role in the Allied war effort. However, it likely would not have prevented the Holocaust entirely, especially in territories rapidly conquered by Nazi Germany. The scale of difference would depend largely on timing, immigration capacity, international recognition, and wartime military realities.

human_answers: Here's a concept for ITTL's N64: yeah yeah it's the same design sue me Name(s): Ultra Nintendo UN/NU (colloquial) Release Date: JP: May 16th, 1998 US: July 4th, 1998 EU: October 24th, 1998 Units Sold: ~20-30 million Amount of Games: ~450 (not including UDD-only titles; including these, ~1,200) Cost: $249 at launch Developers: Nintendo, IBM, ATI Manufacturer: Nintendo CPU: IBM PowerPC 721 (codenamed "Uranium") RCP: ATI Rage Ultra Sound Chip: None; handled by the CPU and RCP RDRAM: 10MB (expandable to 20MB with the Expansion Pak) Media: Cartridges (supported up to 80MB); MiniCDs (only with the UDD; supported up to 208MB) Storage: No internal storage; 32-128KB via official controller paks (upwards of 512KB via third-party paks) Polygon Count: 1-2 million Colors: 16.8 million Resolution: 256x224 to 640x480; supported anamorphic widescreen I tried to make it so it's a mixture of the DreamCast and N64 power- and architecture-wise, as well as adding elements of the GameCube.

It has been a while since I have touched on gaming history, so forgive my error if I make any mistakes here. The failure of the Sega Saturn is kind of exaggerated if you ask me. The Sega Saturn did well in Japan and even outsold the N64 in that region (Although to be fair, N64 sales were not that great in Japan to begin with). The issue with the Sega Saturn is bad marketing (At least for the Western release) and its lack of key brands that sold in the West, namely Sonic (And I mean a real Sonic game like a Sonic equivalent of Sonic the Hedgehog for Sega Genesis or Sonic Adventure for the Dreamcast). The Dreamcast did worse than the Sega Saturn in terms of overall sales, and many people that I have seen treat the Dreamcast like it was almost a smashing success while the Saturn was a total failure with no hope of ever being successful. That said, if Sega gets SGI, then this gives them a big edge. Sega can make 3D games easier, which would mean that it would be easier for them to make a Sonic equivalent of Mario 64 or Spyro the Dragon. A really good 3D Sonic Game that is on par with a game like Sonic Adventure in our timeline, and better marketing could lead to the Sega Saturn being very successful, although probably less so than the PS1. In addition, if Sega maintains a strong Japanese lineup for the Sega Saturn, then this could translate to strong sales in Japan as well as the West. If Sega had this amount of success, then it may still be in business today. I am not sure who Nintendo would partner with instead. They already tried to partner with Sony and Phillips, and their partnership with Sony gave us the PlayStation, while their partnership with Phillips gave us some funny early 2000s memes and YTPS lol. But Nintendo will probably be in a worse overall position, at least in console making, although the Handheld market should still be in their ballpark, seeing how successful the Gameboy and Gameboy Color were.

items.original_question: What If Sega Saturn Adopts SGI Technology: Brainstorming thread. Hi everyone, I'm new to this website, and I wanted to try my hand at making my own alternate timeline. While this one is going to be mainly a video game based timeline, It'll also look at pop culture as a whole, if I can come up with any good ideas. So, here's my pitch. Sega. One of the most well known gaming companies in the world, creators of franchises such as Golden Axe, Virtua Fighter, Phantasy Star, and of course, Sonic The Hedgehog. A big player in the console wars, and the biggest rival to Nintendo. Despite all that, Sega went from making consoles, to being relegated to a third party manufacturer. A series of missteps and poor decisions led to the company struggling in the 5th generation, and not long after, they ended up ceasing console production after the release of the dreamcast. But there was one way they could have managed to keep making consoles. And not just stay in the console market, but change gaming history as we know it... That's right! SGI, the company that helped Nintendo develop the n64, were at one point going to work with Sega instead! Tom Kalinske, Ceo of Sega of America (SoA) at the time, was Approached by SGI who had told him about a chip that they thought would work great for a video game console. Kalinske was impressed by their work and wanted to get approval by Sega of Japan's (SoJ) hardware team to move forward with this deal. SoJ rejected the SGI chip, even after the team had managed to fix the "problems" that Japanese hardware team pointed out, a meeting with SoJ CEO Hayao Nakayama who rejected the chip, killed any chance of SGI working on a Sega Console. SGI would then go on to pitch their technology to Nintendo, who approved of their design, and the rest is history. So with all that out of the way, here's the basic premise for this timeline. What if SGI was not only allowed to work with Sega, but their technology was integrated into the Saturn? I'll be the first to admit, that i'm not the first one to come up with this question. But from what I can tell, no one else has tried to make a full timeline for this concept. So that's where I decided to step in. While I have a general idea of how I want this timeline to pan out, there's still some details I need help with. Which is why I'm making a brainstorming thread. As for what I need help with? Anything to do with console specs would be a major help. As well as trying to figure out who the heck Nintendo would work with for the N64, or whatever they'd call it in this timeline. So to anyone that's reading this, be sure to give me some ideas, I'm all ears.

items.model_answer:
If Sega had adopted SGI (Silicon Graphics) technology for the Saturn, the fifth-generation console race could have unfolded very differently—both technically and commercially.

The core issue with the real Saturn was architectural complexity. Sega designed it primarily as a 2D powerhouse, then hastily bolted on 3D capabilities to compete with Sony’s PlayStation. The result was a dual-CPU system with multiple co-processors that was notoriously difficult to program for. Developers struggled to extract performance, especially for 3D graphics, and many third-party studios prioritized the easier-to-develop-for PlayStation. This complexity, combined with Sega’s surprise early launch and strained developer relations, hurt the Saturn’s market performance.

If Sega had partnered with SGI—whose technology underpinned the Nintendo 64 and who had deep expertise in 3D graphics hardware—the Saturn likely would have launched with a more streamlined, 3D-optimized architecture. SGI’s strengths were in advanced graphics pipelines, floating-point performance, and scalable 3D systems. A Saturn built around SGI principles might have featured a unified graphics architecture better suited to polygons, texture mapping, and 3D environments. That alone could have made it far more competitive against the PlayStation, whose simple, efficient design was one of its greatest strengths.

A more developer-friendly Saturn would have changed the software landscape significantly. Third-party developers such as Square, Namco, and Capcom might have found it easier and more profitable to build for Sega’s platform. In reality, Square famously chose PlayStation over Nintendo 64 partly due to storage limitations and development flexibility; if Sega had offered both CD-ROM storage and strong 3D performance in an accessible architecture, it might have attracted major exclusives like Final Fantasy VII or retained stronger long-term third-party loyalty. Sega already had respected arcade franchises, and pairing them with superior or equal 3D console hardware could have given it a powerful content advantage.

Commercially, a competitive SGI-based Saturn might have prevented Sony’s rapid dominance. The PlayStation succeeded not just because of technology, but because it hit a sweet spot: affordable, powerful, and easy to develop for. If Sega had matched that technical accessibility while leveraging its existing brand recognition and arcade credibility, the fifth generation might have become a true three-way race among Sega, Sony, and Nintendo instead of a PlayStation-driven shift in industry power. Sega’s financial decline in the late 1990s—exacerbated by Saturn’s poor performance—might have been avoided, potentially preventing the need for the Dreamcast to serve as a high-risk comeback console.

However, there are constraints to consider. SGI technology, especially in the mid-1990s, was associated with high-end workstations and was not cheap. Nintendo’s partnership with SGI resulted in powerful but expensive hardware, and the Nintendo 64’s cost structure influenced decisions like sticking with cartridges. If Sega had adopted a similar approach, the Saturn might have been more expensive at launch, undermining its competitiveness. Sony’s aggressive pricing was crucial to its success. If SGI-based hardware pushed Sega’s retail price too high, the benefits of better 3D capability might have been offset by weaker adoption.

In the broader historical arc, a successful SGI-powered Saturn could have preserved Sega as a top-tier hardware manufacturer into the 2000s. That might have altered the dynamics of the sixth generation as well: the Dreamcast might not have been necessary in its eventual form, Microsoft’s Xbox entry might have faced a stronger established competitor, and Sony’s path to near-hegemony in the early 2000s could have been slowed. The industry might have remained more evenly balanced, with Sega continuing to shape console innovation rather than exiting hardware in 2001.

In short, adopting SGI technology could have given Sega a technically coherent, 3D-focused Saturn that competed far more effectively with the PlayStation. While not guaranteeing victory—pricing, marketing, and business strategy still mattered enormously—it likely would have prevented the Saturn from becoming the commercial misstep that precipitated Sega’s withdrawal from the console hardware market.

items.question: What If Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004
human_answers: Another Daschle term would have been a real step down for Democrats in terms of leadership. Reid and Pelosi were the best Democratic floor leaders in generations and having them commanding the two chambers at the same time is a very big part of why Obama's first two years were so damn productive. Daschle rose through the ranks because he was really good on TV. Reid was terrible on camera, so Daschle is a plus for Democrats here, but I'm not sure it really matters. W was so badly screwing up his second term that Dems didn't really need to convince anyone that things were on the wrong track. The really interesting Qs are what Dems would do with an extra vote's breathing room in the Senate -- is it enough for Daschle to actually get things done even if he's less of a vote-counter than Reid? -- and what impact Daschle's somewhat more expansionist personal opinion on healthcare reform does to Obamacare. Daschle's tax fraud stemmed from income he earned from 2005-2007 -- i.e, after he lost re-election. He won't have that job or that income in ATL, so the whole scandal is butterflied away.

I don't see anyone mentioning the biggest butterfly: Ted Kennedy. Ted Kennedy died in August (I think?) taking Dems down to 59 seats. That's not going to happen if there's an extra seat. They're not going to have to bargain with Ben Nelson to get anything through. Dems are going to be at 60 seats through 2010. Also consequential, they're going to beat 60 seats before March of 2009 because of Al Franken. They had to do a run-off election which meant the Obama administration had to wait an extra 2-3 months to get their super majority. Daschle-Reid were effective. They got Jim Jeffords to switch. They'll be able to get something passed. Daschle wrote a book about how how single-payer is the ideal system but it's problematic in the states. I expect him to push for some Federal Health Board which will only increase death panel comparisons. I'd be interested in what others thing they can get passed through 2009-2010. More stimulus. More infrastructure. I'd love to hear thoughts. There's a small miracle that Daschle can survive in 2010 especially if he's up against a Tea Party lunatic. It's forgotten now but there was some talk after 2012 post-Sandy Hook that Obama might be the rare President who makes gains in the sixth year midterms. I think that's a stretch but it's not inconceivable. If Daschle can convince the retiring Senate Democrats to stay they certainly don't need to lose 9 seats.

Daschle loosing was a real bit of mud in the eye for Democrats in 2004. Him squeaking through would have been a help for sure; anything that gives Democrats an extra vote in the Senate in 2008-2010 will be a big help for Obama's agenda and the ACA. I don't remember how effective he was as a senate leader, Reid wasn't exactly a slouch though. He also had a corruption scandal in 2009 which might become a bigger deal if he's Senate majority leader. Big picture wise, the question is does the extra vote in the Senate and easier passage of a stronger ACA snowball into a more successful presidency for Obama? There's still going to be backlash in 2010, but if more gets done in 2008-2010 thanks to a less intransigent senate, then that momentum could carry forwards. Do they try to do immigration reform, or a stronger recovery package if less of the oxygen is sucked up by healthcare? Big picture the country would have all the same fundamental issues it currently does, but if the vibes are shifted enough in 2016 things could get very different, especially if a certain Orange man decides to stay out of the race.
items.original_question: What if Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004 Tom Daschle was a Democratic senator from South Dakota who served as the Senate Democratic Caucus leader from 1995 to 2005. In 2004, Daschle was defeated by Republican John Thune by a narrow margin of only 4,508 votes. Daschle would be succeeded as the Senate Democratic leader by Harry Reid of Nevada, who would go on to serve as Senate Majority Leader during the last two years of George W. Bush’s second term and the first two years of Barack Obama’s first term. Democrats would achieve a supermajority during Obama’s first term, enabling the passage of the Affordable Care Act. However, the presence of Senator Joe Lieberman in the Democratic caucus would frustrate Obama’s agenda, axing the public option from the ACA. However, had Tom Daschle won re-election in 2004, perhaps Daschle would have been the 60th vote instead of Joe Lieberman. And unlike Lieberman, Daschle would very likely be for the public option. What would be the impact of a public option being passed as part of ObamaCare? What might change in the 2006, 2008, and 2010 elections if Daschle continued to lead the Democrats rather than Harry Reid? Would Democrats still win all of the seats they would win IOTL?

items.model_answer:
If Tom Daschle had won re‑election to the U.S. Senate from South Dakota in 2004, several meaningful political consequences likely would have followed, both for the Senate and for Democratic Party strategy.

First, the immediate balance of power in the Senate would have shifted slightly. In reality, Daschle’s loss to John Thune gave Republicans a 55–45 majority in the 109th Congress. If Daschle had won, Republicans would likely have held 54 seats instead. While still a majority, it would have been somewhat narrower, making party unity even more critical for advancing President George W. Bush’s agenda. On closely contested issues—such as Social Security privatization, judicial confirmations, and Iraq War policy—a stronger and experienced Democratic leader could have sharpened opposition and possibly altered the legislative trajectory at the margins.

Second, Daschle’s personal role would have been significant. As Senate Democratic Leader (a position he held before his defeat), he would likely have continued shaping national Democratic strategy. Daschle was seen as pragmatic and institutionally focused, often favoring negotiation over confrontation. His continued leadership might have tempered some of the sharper partisan escalation that developed in the mid‑2000s, though polarization was already well underway. At the same time, his survival would have symbolized Democratic resilience in a difficult election year, potentially strengthening party morale.

Third, his presence could have influenced Democratic positioning heading into the 2006 midterms. Democrats ultimately regained control of Congress in 2006 under leaders like Harry Reid and Nancy Pelosi. With Daschle still in the Senate, leadership dynamics might have differed. He could have remained leader or transitioned to a senior statesman role, shaping messaging around Iraq, health care, and fiscal policy. His Midwestern profile might also have helped the party maintain stronger connections to rural and Plains-state voters.

Finally, Daschle’s later career trajectory would have changed. After his 2004 defeat, he moved into policy and lobbying circles and was later nominated (unsuccessfully) by President Obama to be Secretary of Health and Human Services. Had he remained in the Senate, he might have played a direct legislative role in crafting the Affordable Care Act rather than being considered for an executive appointment.

Overall, a Daschle victory in 2004 would not have radically transformed U.S. politics, but it would have modestly narrowed Republican control, preserved an experienced Democratic leader during a pivotal period, and potentially altered Senate leadership dynamics and legislative negotiations in the Bush administration’s second term.

items.question: Beauty of a Red Star: What If the Soviets Landed on the Moon
human_answers: 13/12/2025 Lyamtsino, Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic, U.S.S.R. School was something I never really struggled at. I knew many kids, many soon-to-be model citizens, and those delinquents who would always ask for the homework assignment they missed because of some laundry list of excuses. I didn’t mind though, as long as they were happy, got what they wanted, and they left me alone, it was just the way things worked and I didn’t feel the need to come in like an American and tear the whole structure down! As long as the people were happy, I could just enjoy the little free time the school provided. This particular day, I was sitting in the little library my school had. It had many works, most of them related to the great soviets achievements and literature of our time, though that was mostly taught in our labour class. It was an easy thing to memorize, the men seemed to really only focus on the hard physical theory while the girls on the more intellectual ones… what was I saying? Oh! The library! I remember browsing the selection of books they had. One caught my eyes, I don’t remember the exact title but it was something like ‘The Cosmos’. Now the thing about this book was that it was entirely in English. Which was strange, it shouldnt've been at the time, we had many books in many languages! My school growing up was one of the more diverse ones in Russia, we had a Kazakh teacher, I remember one of my friends was Armenian, I even met a few Ukrainians and Poles. Oh sorry, right the book! I looked at the pages, I didn’t understand most of it, English wasn’t really taught at my younger age… At least I don’t think so. I brought the book up to the first teacher I saw. “Maria Ivanovna!” I asked, I remember her old boney face, She must’ve been teaching there since Stalin was around. She adjusted her glasses, those beady brown eyes bearing down on me. “Irina Serebryákova, what is it?” I am not sure if she was disinterested or merely tired, I would be tired too if I had to teach the same group of students for years and years. Holding up the book, I flipped through the pages showing the text inside, and looking at her confused old face I remember saying, “What is this about! Why is it in English?” “It is about space.” She snatched the book, adjusting her glasses as she skimmed the pages, “The cosmos... in the eyes of the west.” “The west?" I asked, she could probably have seen my innocent gaze, that look of confusion as I followed it up, "I didn’t know they thought differently about that.” The old woman scoffed a bit, setting the book down, “In every aspect they do, it’s not an ideological thing, it’s the very core of their beliefs. The societies that make up the west only understand science as a means of capital.” At the time I wasn’t sure what she entirely meant. America and her friends were the enemy, ideologically we oppose each other at every turn, but science? Wasn’t that something every nation agrees on? “Remember, Irina Serebryákova, there is a reason we landed on the moon .” There is a reason. There’s always a reason for something. After that I don’t remember much, I think I thanked her and went on my way, I had stayed a little later and began walking home. We landed on the moon, yes, and what I was told the world celebrated. But was that not really the case? My younger self was struggling with these odd ideas… and I know it should’ve been more obvious, but I am older, and you think about things differently. Like how when I was younger I had a crush on… Oh, I am sorry, I’m rambling again. Can we take a short break?
items.original_question: Beauty of a Red Star: What if the Soviets Landed on the Moon “What seemed impossible yesterday is now a task for tomorrow.” - Sergei Korolev ​ It has been quite a while since I have posted anything in this section, and that is mostly because I don't really consider myself a huge writer. However, this timeline idea has been stuck in my head, and I wanted to finally put it into action. For the full experience please go into Reader Mode! What is this timeline? The basic premise is that the American Apollo Program experiences significantly more delays and problems than OTL along with smaller things I won't spoil, and the Soviets manage to send a rocket and land in 1971. Now I want to say out the gate, the landing itself isn't realistic. Realism isn't the point of the divergence. The timeline won't be focusing on major historical figures, while there will be snippets of people like Nixon, they are not the center piece. What will this timeline focus on? Unlike other timelines, the focus, for the most part, isn't about the space race and getting to the moon. It is about the aftermath and how the world is altered. Is this like For All Mankind? Would you believe me if I said I have never seen the show? But I assume any TL about the Soviets landing on the moon will have some similarities. When are Updates? Seeing I am in university and have not the best health, it will not have a set thing. I already have a few pre-made things ready, but please just be patient with me.

items.model_answer:
If the Soviet Union had landed cosmonauts on the Moon before the United States, the event would have reshaped not only the space race but also the political psychology of the Cold War. The Moon landing was never just a technical milestone; it was a global symbol of ideological superiority. A Soviet victory would have given communism a dramatic, visual triumph at the very moment television was turning space exploration into shared human spectacle.

First, the political impact would have been immediate and intense. The United States had framed Apollo as proof of the vitality of liberal democracy and free-market innovation. A Soviet landing—especially if achieved in the late 1960s—would have been interpreted worldwide as evidence that centralized planning and socialist science could outperform American capitalism. In the developing world, where many nations were choosing between alignment with Washington or Moscow, this symbolic win could have strengthened pro-Soviet movements and bolstered socialist parties. It would not necessarily have converted the West to communism, but it would have weakened the aura of American inevitability.

Domestically in the United States, the shock might have resembled a more profound version of the “Sputnik moment” of 1957. Congress would likely have poured even more resources into NASA, perhaps accelerating plans for Mars missions or permanent lunar bases. The political backlash could have deepened Cold War hawkishness, increasing military and technological competition. Alternatively, it might have triggered earlier calls for détente, especially if policymakers feared the escalating costs of symbolic rivalry.

For the Soviet Union itself, a lunar landing would have been a crowning achievement for its scientific establishment. The prestige boost could have strengthened the legitimacy of the Communist Party during a period when economic stagnation was beginning to set in. Yet it is unlikely that one triumph—even one as grand as the Moon—would have reversed deeper structural problems in the Soviet economy. The systemic inefficiencies that contributed to the USSR’s eventual collapse in 1991 were rooted in long-term economic and political constraints that a single technological victory could not erase.

Culturally, the imagery of a red flag on the Moon would have reshaped global imagination. Instead of Neil Armstrong’s “one small step,” schoolchildren worldwide might have memorized the words of a Soviet cosmonaut. Space exploration narratives—films, textbooks, museum exhibits—would have been anchored in a Soviet first. The symbolic association between space and American identity would have been weaker, and international space cooperation might have taken a different path, perhaps with the USSR in a stronger leadership role in setting norms for lunar exploration.

In the long run, however, the structural dynamics of the Cold War likely would have reasserted themselves. The United States possessed greater economic depth and technological flexibility, while the Soviet Union faced mounting internal strains. A Soviet Moon landing would have been a stunning and beautiful triumph—a red star shining over the Sea of Tranquility—but it probably would not have altered the ultimate trajectory of superpower rivalry. It would have changed the story of who first touched another world, and for a generation that story would have mattered enormously, even if history’s deeper currents continued to flow in much the same direction.

items.question: What If Germany had secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade in World War II?
human_answers: The RN and other allies can only block the marine trade, so the first thing is to look at who Germany has land borders with. Then, which of those countries might have food or other essentials that Germany needs. If these are willing and able to trade [1], then Germany can maybe get by but if not then they either make do or try to take things by force. Nazi Germany chose force instead of negotiation and trade to try to beak the blockade. Why? because their leaders were mad bastards who were completely untrustworthy to trade with, thought they were better than everyone else, thought that violent conflict was good and who wanted to take over Russian lands for themselves: it ended badly. [1] Italy, for example, might have been willing to trade with Germany, but getting goods into Italy by sea is difficult with the British blocking imports intended for or suspected to be intended for Germany.

Yes its difficult to imagine it now but in 1939 the British had a near monopoly on merchant shipping and many nations merchant ships and their cargos would be 'under written' that is insured by British firms. And much of a nations cargos would likely travel on British ships or ships owned by British firms. In WW1 the blockade of Germany had been part physical i.e. warships stopping ships and inspecting cargos and manifests etc and part commercial pressure. Indeed it was discovered that many of the cargos that had been going to Germany pre war were instead going to Neutral nations like the Netherlands and Denmark and simply continuing on to Germany overland. By 1915 this 'loop hole' was effectively stopped using the commercial apparatus to quite simply restrict goods to no more than had been going to those neutral nations before the war meaning that very little would be left to sell on to Germany.

items.model_answer:
If Germany had secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade, the strategic trajectory of World War II would likely have shifted significantly—but not automatically toward a German victory.

The Allied blockade was a central pillar of Britain’s war strategy. Germany historically suffered chronic shortages of oil, fats, grain, and especially natural rubber, forcing heavy reliance on synthetic substitutes and territorial conquest (Romanian oil, Ukrainian grain). These shortages constrained mobility, limited training and air operations, weakened civilian morale, and forced risky offensives aimed at resource capture—most notably the invasion of the Soviet Union with its eye on Caucasian oil. If Germany had secured reliable external supplies—through guaranteed access to neutral markets, protected sea lanes, or a stable Eurasian resource network—the strategic pressure driving many of its most desperate decisions would have eased.

With abundant oil, the Wehrmacht could have sustained longer air campaigns, expanded pilot training, and maintained mechanized offensives without the chronic fuel rationing that crippled operations after 1942. The Luftwaffe’s declining pilot quality and sortie rates were closely tied to fuel scarcity. A well-fueled German military would have been more capable of prolonged strategic bombing, stronger defense against Allied air superiority, and more resilient responses during campaigns such as North Africa and the Eastern Front.

Reliable rubber supplies would have strengthened vehicle production and maintenance, increasing logistical flexibility. Food security would have reduced domestic strain and improved morale, potentially limiting labor unrest and the need for harsh extraction policies in occupied territories that fueled resistance movements.

Most consequentially, with secure oil supplies, Germany might not have needed to prioritize the 1942 drive toward the Caucasus or overextend itself in resource-driven offensives. A Germany less constrained by scarcity might have fought a more defensive, attritional war after early victories—consolidating gains in Europe and forcing the Allies into a longer, more costly reconquest.

However, several constraints would still remain. First, industrial capacity: by 1943–44, the United States vastly outproduced Germany in ships, aircraft, vehicles, and munitions. Even without resource shortages, Germany faced an overwhelming material imbalance. Second, Allied codebreaking, strategic bombing, and growing Soviet manpower would still exert enormous pressure. Third, ideological and strategic miscalculations—such as the decision to invade the Soviet Union and the genocidal occupation policies that fueled partisan warfare—were not simply products of resource scarcity.

In the best-case scenario for Germany, sustainable supplies might have prolonged the war considerably, possibly forcing a negotiated settlement in Europe if Allied casualties mounted and public support wavered. A more stable German war economy could have delayed collapse on both Eastern and Western fronts, perhaps preventing the rapid disintegration of 1944–45.

But outright Axis victory would still have required defeating or neutralizing both the Soviet Union and the United States—an enormous task even with adequate resources. American industrial supremacy and Soviet manpower reserves were structural advantages that resource sufficiency alone would not erase.

In sum, a Germany free from blockade-induced shortages would likely have fought longer, more effectively, and at greater cost to the Allies. The war might have extended years beyond 1945 or ended in a negotiated division of Europe. Yet resource security, while critical, would not automatically overcome the deep economic and strategic asymmetries that ultimately determined the war’s outcome.

items.question: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?
human_answers: Well, according to Google "Canada's first CANDU prototype, the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor, required a significant amount of heavy water (D2O) for its moderator and coolant, generally around 1 tonne of heavy water per megawatt (MW) of capacity, translating to roughly 20-25 tonnes for its small 20 MWe output..." and "In the 1930's Norwegian company Norsk Hydro began industrial-scale extraction of heavy water (deuterium oxide) at its Vemork plant in Rjukan, using electrolysis as a byproduct of fertilizer production, " Finally from Wikipedia (yes, I know this may well be nonsense) "It was the world's first site to mass-produce heavy water (as a byproduct of nitrogen fixing), with a capacity of 1.2 tonnes per year. " So, by the late 1930's / early 1940's it might well be possible to build a 1 or 2MW CANDU stream generator using just one or two years production from the single Norsk Hydro plant. I assume Canadian hydro plants were built with higher capacity since they (the Canadians) managed to build commercial output (GW) plants requiring 200-300 tones of heavy water in a 'reasonable' timescale (ie. less than 200 years )

Believe it or not, my first engineering degree was in Nuclear Engineering (it was a dead field when I graduated 30 plus years ago, and still is, so I got another degree in Manufacturing Engineering). Yes, you can run reactors with natural enrichment, and the right neutron moderator - heavy water (as in the water molecules have Deuterium instead of your usual one proton no neutrons hydrogen) or graphite come to mind. Both would avoid the need to enrich the fuel (which is a major hassle to do). BUT, that's only part of the story - you need the instrumentation for monitoring the nuclear reactions (to make sure they're occurring, and not getting out of control) which is basically electronic in nature (sorry mechanical won't cut it). In the early 1900s, the field of electronics was embryonic at best. Then there's the material science aspect - you need materials seriously capable of dealing with the high reactor temperatures, and radiation effects (oh yeah, and the material can't interfere excessively with the neutron flux, which would disrupt the reaction) - sorry not happening, material science was in its infancy IMO. There is also the safety aspect - you need shielding for any radiation emitted from the reactor. The health aspects of radiation exposure were basically unknown, resulting in many people getting exposed to and dying of cancer (Marie Curie, early X-Ray technicians, the so called "Radium Girls" who painted the glowing dots on watch faces). In certain cases of extreme exposure (due to reactor surges, etc.), you can die from the radiation days after the exposure. In short, IMO, having a viable nuclear reactor in the early 1900s is a non-starter.

To your first part: Fair enough. It seems like this might require ASB, like just magically gifting people the entire lexicon of nuclear understanding and teaching them how to make purer graphite. I'm not sure I entirely agree with the second part. Were the engineers that built the Chicago Pile doing sophisticated core analysis? Did they know the neutron flux? I feel like you could "fly blind" and just go by heat/steam output, especially since "won't immediately melt down and ruin my investment" is probably considered sufficient by 1900s standards of safety (especially if the health effects of radiation are not yet understood). Granted, it seems very, very likely that the long term effects of this mentality would make for a much more radioactively contaminated world... Ah, but I didn't say for generating electricity, per se. A nuclear boiler just for steam would be useful. And I doubt they'd come up with a design that requires steam generators or controlling boron concentration in the coolant: I wouldn't expect anything like a PWR with its separation between a primary and secondary loop. More like a BWR or RBMK, where the radioactive steam is directly used. If the objective is electricity, it may require a bit longer than early 1900s. But by the time you have coal plants coming online, you have everything you need for the conventional thermal plant.

To elaborate on some things: as far as I can tell, there are possibly 3 historical reactor designs that used unenriched/natural uranium: heavy-water moderated CANDU reactors, graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors (Magnox and UNGG), and possibly the graphite-moderated Soviet RBMK reactors (although RBMK reactors typically used low-enriched uranium). Heavy water's out of the question; it was only discovered in the 1930s, and even WW2-era methods for extracting heavy water were massively energy-intensive. NPD, the first CANDU reactor producing some 20 MW of electricity, required 28,660kg of heavy water. Using pure electrolysis to extract the heavy water - the initial method used to extract heavy water at Vemork - required about 58,000 kilowatt hours per pound of heavy water, or 3.6 billion kilowatt-hours to produce all the necessary heavy water. As a quick comparison, the US' entire monthly electricity generation in April 1922 was about 3.6 billion kilowatt hours. That means the NPD reactor, if it obtained heavy water using pre-WW2 methods, could run for 20 years straight and not break even on the power needed to create the heavy water necessary to run the plant (not to mention some heavy water will be lost in operation) before the development of postwar heavy water production methods. UNGG and RBMK definitely used zirconium cladding for their fuel elements (necessary because zirconium has a smaller neutron absorption cross-section and is resistant to corrosion); the issue is that metal zirconium wasn't commercially synthesized until 1925, and it wasn't commercially synthesized cheaply until after WW2. The specific zirconium alloys used in the fuel claddings weren't developed until the postwar either. RBMK reactors operate with water at pressures of about 1,000 psi; that wasn't achieved by land-based power generation systems until 1925. Uranium metal used in the gas-cooled reactors is difficult to work with considering it corrodes a lot of metals when molten, thus requiring graphite molds of decently high purity (maybe not as pure as nuclear graphite, but boron has to be minimized). Also the furnaces used to cast the uranium were vacuum induction furnaces, a technology not invented until the 1920s. Turning the uranium metal into fuel rods that can be inserted also required a ton of research and development to the point where it was once considered the most critical job at Hanford for the Manhattan Project.
items.original_question: What if A nuclear reactor, four decades early? I posit that with the technology of the early 1900s, a nuclear reactor could've been theoretically possible had the theory been understood. Uranium enrichment is entirely out of the question, but not all reactor designs require it. The industrialists of the 1900s had access to graphite, yellowcake, and boron, which would allow the creation and control of a graphite-moderated natural uranium reactor, so long as the graphite was pure enough (I am admittedly unsure if that level of purity would be possible, but I am presuming so given what little I know of the process). Is there any plausible scenario where the discovery of nuclear fission is pushed back far enough for our enterprising titans of industry to begin harnessing nuclear steam, short of dropping off a modern nuclear physics textbook in their engineers' laps? If so, what effects would this have on the world?

items.model_answer:
If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around 1900, the political, military, and economic trajectory of the 20th century would likely have changed dramatically—but not in a simple or uniformly transformative way.

First, the scientific and industrial context matters. Around 1900, physics was still developing the foundations of atomic theory. Even if fission had been identified and chain reactions engineered, scaling reactors would have required advances in materials science, precision engineering, and large-scale industrial coordination. The most likely early adopters would have been major industrial powers—Britain, Germany, France, and the United States—because they had the scientific institutions and capital required. Nuclear power would initially have been state-driven and tightly linked to military and naval ambitions.

One immediate impact would likely have been on naval power. Coal was central to imperial logistics; fleets depended on coaling stations across empires. Nuclear-powered ships—even if primitive—would have radically reduced refueling needs and altered the strategic value of colonial ports. The British Empire, whose power relied heavily on coal logistics, might have retained naval supremacy longer if it mastered nuclear propulsion early. Alternatively, if Germany gained an early lead, it could have shifted the naval balance before World War I.

World War I itself could have unfolded differently. If reactors existed by the 1910s, they might initially have served as stationary power sources for industry and rail electrification rather than weapons. However, once fission was understood, the possibility of atomic bombs would have followed sooner or later. Given the intense arms race atmosphere before 1914, there is a real possibility that nuclear weapons research would have begun during or immediately after World War I. If atomic bombs had appeared in the 1910s or 1920s, their first use might have been in a far less restrained strategic culture than that of 1945. The norms and taboos that developed after Hiroshima did not exist earlier, and mass bombing of civilians was already becoming normalized during World War I. An earlier nuclear age might therefore have been even more destabilizing.

Economically, early nuclear power could have reduced dependence on coal decades earlier. This might have slowed the growth of oil geopolitics, potentially reducing the strategic centrality of the Middle East. Electrification could have expanded faster, especially in Europe, if reactors provided abundant base-load power. On the other hand, early reactors would likely have been expensive and centralized, reinforcing state control over energy rather than democratizing it.

In terms of environmental effects, earlier nuclear adoption might have reduced cumulative carbon emissions over the 20th century by displacing some coal burning. However, without modern safety culture and regulatory frameworks, accidents and radiation exposure could have been more frequent and poorly managed, possibly creating public backlash or localized disasters.

Politically, the existence of nuclear weapons before or during World War I could have either deterred large-scale war or made it catastrophically shorter and more destructive. If one power achieved a temporary monopoly, it might have reshaped the international order decisively—perhaps preventing the prolonged stalemate of trench warfare but at the cost of immense destruction in a few cities. Alternatively, rapid proliferation among rival empires could have made preemptive war more likely in a highly unstable multipolar system.

Overall, an early discovery of practical fission around 1900 would probably have accelerated both the centralization of state power and the scale of destructive capability. The 20th century might have seen nuclear geopolitics emerge not after two world wars but before or during the first—potentially making the era either more quickly stabilized through deterrence or even more violently transformative in its opening decades.

items.question: Skywalker Ranch Foundation: What If Lucasfilm Was Never Sold to Disney
human_answers: Lucas didn’t expend much effort in assembling the rest of the Creative Council. It was mostly a collection of people who had defined Lucasfilm properties for a generation. The first member was Kiri Hart, Lucasfilm’s resident surveyor of canon. Doug Chiang was the second to agree. He had created the stunning visual spectacles that were Naboo and Coruscant in The Phantom Menace. He had made the prequels more mythic in appearance than the originals and that was someone Filoni felt this new Foundation needed. Kathleen Kennedy was the last member. She had overseen the creation of many classics, mostly outside of Lucasfilm. Even if that wasn’t the case, Filoni could not pretend there wasn’t a corporate aspect to the Foundation. The corporation was what would keep the Foundation propped up. Filoni felt both eager to get underway and terrified about what would happen in this meeting. Lucas had essentially anointed him his successor. There was a lot to live up to, but Filoni trusted Lucas’ judgement and that was the only consolation he could come up with. Filoni walked into the boardroom and he clapped his hands. “Hey, everyone. Thank you for coming”, he said. The creators nodded in Filoni’s direction as he sat down. Doug pushed his notepad to the centre of the desk as Kiri closed her binder full of canon notes. “I know what you’re thinking. This is new territory for me too. But, let’s see how this pans out”, Filoni replied. The creators didn’t respond. “Our mandate is clear. We have the responsibility to protect what Lucasfilm stands for. We need to tell new stories while protecting what the old ones stand for”, As some of the creators shifted position in their seats, Dave continued. “This is about the generations of people who see Lucasfilm as the pillar of mythic entertainment”, he said. “What do we do first?” Kennedy asked. “The Foundation goes public in October. Before then, I want a clear statement of what the Foundation will stand for. We don’t want our fans to have any doubt about our integrity”, Kiri nodded, but asked. “What is our integrity? What do we stand for?” Dave looked around the table. “We stand for storytelling and for what it can bring to the world”, he said. “That is a noble goal, Dave. But we can’t forget that part of this Foundation is a business. We need to operate within current and upcoming industries. We need to form connections”, Kennedy replied. Doug then replied. “I don’t think Dave is forgetting that, but we need to tell the industry that we decide what stories are told. Too many stories are being decided in high rise boardrooms”, Filoni nodded. “Exactly. There is a balance we need to respect”, he said. “Creative sovereignty will be our first pillar then. We will work with the industry, but we won’t let them rewrite our stories to fit social media trends”, Kiri replied. Dave nodded in her direction. “We also need to figure out a commercially viable way to support new creators. Are we going to let everyone with a camera and dream camp outside of Skywalker Ranch and hope for their shot?” Kennedy asked. “Once we work out that process, how do we protect their work?” she continued. “Okay, so we’ve decided on our values. Creative sovereignty, visual and emotional integrity and creator support”, Dave said as he counted the values on his fingers. “Who wants to work on the statement?” he called out. Kiri and Doug stood up. “We’ll get it started”, Dave nodded as he looked at Kennedy. “I’ll get the production framework going”, she said. Filoni laid back in his seat. This first meeting was remarkably painless, but he suspected this was where the ease of the job ended. Comments We are a long way off from dealing with the sequels, but they will be addressed eventually. I will be preserving the Mandalorian, since that was Filoni's pet project for a while. And yes, Lucasfilm will be retaining their relationship with Disney. If there is something like Galaxy's Edge, it won't be entirely based around the sequels.
items.original_question: Skywalker Ranch Foundation: What if Lucasfilm Was Never Sold to Disney (I originally intended for this to be a timeline which would've covered the production of a Clone Wars-style animated series set in a different version of the sequel trilogy, but when I determined that Disney was too business oriented to create something like what I was making, I went back to the drawing board and I came up with this instead. This will be my first production timeline so I may or may not update this on the regular, but I wanted to do something to mark the 10th anniversary of The Force Awakens) Anyway, sound off on what you think. # June 2012 “Well done, everybody!” Dave Filoni shouted when he saw the final animation of The Wrong Jedi, the last episode of The Clone Wars Season 5. There was loud applause from across the room. Filoni looked back towards George Lucas. He could’ve sworn he saw a tear in the old man’s eye. The Clone Wars was out for another season. The final step was to send the seasons to Cartoon Network to show the fans. Filoni thought this was probably the best season yet. He wasn’t surprised since he knew he had the best team in the business working alongside him. But, the celebration couldn’t last forever. He had to work with his team on the next season. Lucas had been a felt absence through the production of Season 5, but he had his input on scripts he thought were special. Filoni smiled as he wondered how long he could keep luring Lucas back to Skywalker Ranch. Before the team could leave, Lucas called out. “Before you leave, I have an announcement to make”, he said. The team turned to face Lucas, but Lucas raised his hand. “Not here. Let’s go somewhere less shadowy”, he said. Lucas led his team out of the Ranch proper and towards the artificially created lake that sat in the middle of the Skywalker Ranch complex. Filoni was never tired of the verdant paradise that Skywalker Ranch was. “Alright, George. What’s up?” Filoni asked with a brief smile. Lucas looked to his fellow creators and took a deep breath. “I don’t know what to say, so I am just going to come right out and say it. I will be stepping down from Lucasfilm at the end of the year”, The creators looked at each other. Lucas’s felt absence suddenly made sense. There was no shock or gasp of surprise. Instead, there was a quiet acknowledgement. “Are you sure you want that?” Filoni asked. “Yes. I’ve been thinking about it for about a year. I’ve told my stories and I want to spend the rest of my life with my family”, “Who’s going to take over?” Kliner asked. “Kathleen Kennedy is going to be handling the corporate side of things, but that’s not why I called you here”, Lucas continued. The shock of the news that one of Spielberg’s top collaborators was going to run Lucasfilm briefly subsided as they waited for Lucas. “I’ve been considering what to do with this alliance that I’ve spent the better part of my life putting together. When I first built this place, I had just dodged a bullet when A New Hope smashed the box office. I’ve put my life and my psyche on the line to not only make art for people to enjoy, but to make an environment where filmmakers can tell their stories”, Lucas said as he stretched out his arms to take in the entirety of the Ranch. “You’ve certainly accomplished that”, Athena Portillo said to everyone’s agreement. “I’ve considered selling all of this to Disney. They have reach that I can only dream of, but I’ve had my doubts”, he said as he turned around from the lake. “When I first became a filmmaker, I hated the studio system. They were all hacks who made films based on what was popular at the time. I’m not saying Disney is a company full of hacks, but I don’t want their corporate attitudes diluting what I, Gary, Ralph, Ben and Maria created thirty years ago. I want this place to remain pure”, Lucas continued. “I’m sorry, George, but what are you trying to say?” Kliner asked. Lucas exhaled. “I’ve talked with Kathy and Brennan. They were reluctant at first, but they’ve agreed to keep Lucasfilm as an independent entity. Not only that, but they’ve agreed to begin laying the groundwork for the Skywalker Ranch Foundation”, “And what is that?” Filoni asked. “It is what is going to keep Lucasfilm in the public consciousness for the next decade or so. It is going to protect the integrity of everything we’ve made here. Not just Star Wars, but Indiana Jones, Willow and everything else that has this place’s name on it. Nobody will be able to touch the properties inside this building until they can prove they can do the work necessary to preserve it”, Before the creators could ask further questions, Lucas continued. “But the Foundation will also produce new content that fits what this place stands for. We’re still putting the infrastructure together, but it will produce new content outside of the studio system, just like back when the original trilogy was being produced”, “Who’s going to lead this Foundation?” Filoni asked. “Like I said, Kathy is going to lead the corporate side of it, but she won’t be the voice of the Foundation. The Foundation will be led by creators”, Lucas replied. He then looked towards Dave and walked towards him. “When you first joined Lucasfilm in 2008, I was surprised by how connected you were to what this company stood for. You weren’t just a director, you were a storyteller through and through. That’s the kind of person I need keeping the Ranch intact. I want you to be the first leader of the Creative Council”, Dave felt his cheeks turning red. He suddenly felt like he had been pulled back in time to when he first joined Lucasfilm. He thought that had been a joke at first. This didn’t feel like a joke. This was something Dave couldn’t put into words. “You want me to be in charge of your legacy? George, I’m flattered, but that’s a whole different thing from making a TV show”, Dave pointed out. “Just keep the story straight. That will be your job. You will have other creators working alongside you on the Council and these people will stay on to help you in the trenches”, Lucas reassured him as he pointed to the creators, some of whom Filoni had known since he first joined the company. The creators watched as Dave looked out across the water. He could’ve sworn Binary Sunset was playing in the back of his head. This was his threshold. He thought he had crossed that line in 2008, but he had been wrong. Lucas wasn’t just trusting him with his story, he was trusting him with what Lucasfilm was going to stand for after he was gone. Dave separated himself from the real world for a moment. He saw X Wings and TIE Fighters flying over the Ranch, he could hear the ethereal hum of lightsabers and finally, he heard Yoda’s famous phrase. “Do or do not. There is no try”, Filoni turned around. “I’ll do it”, he said which led to applause from his fellow creators and Lucas shaking his hand. “Lucasfilm couldn’t be in better hands”, Lucas simply said.

items.model_answer:
If Lucasfilm had never been sold to Disney in 2012, the trajectory of both *Star Wars* and the broader media landscape would likely look very different. Under continued independent ownership—presumably still guided by George Lucas or a closely aligned creative leadership structure—Lucasfilm would probably have remained a smaller, more creatively centralized studio focused on long-term storytelling rather than rapid franchise expansion.

First, the sequel trilogy as released (Episodes VII–IX) almost certainly would not exist in its current form. George Lucas had his own outlines for sequels centered more on midichlorians, the Whills, and the rebuilding of the Republic. These concepts were reportedly more philosophical and exploratory than the nostalgia-driven approach Disney adopted. Without Disney’s corporate mandate for a tentpole revival, any continuation of the saga would likely have been slower, more experimental, and potentially more divisive—but also more unified in vision.

Second, the scale and speed of franchise expansion would have been far smaller. Disney turned *Star Wars* into a multi-platform streaming ecosystem with series like *The Mandalorian*, *Andor*, *Ahsoka*, and others feeding Disney+. An independent Lucasfilm might have produced occasional films or high-quality television projects, but not at the volume or frequency seen after 2015. The brand would likely feel less saturated and more event-driven, with longer gaps between major releases.

Third, merchandising and global integration would be less aggressive. Disney’s synergy machine—theme park expansions like Galaxy’s Edge, extensive cross-brand licensing, and global marketing saturation—dramatically expanded *Star Wars* as a commercial empire. Without that infrastructure, the franchise would still be lucrative but less omnipresent in global consumer culture. It might retain more of a niche, cult-epic identity rather than functioning as a pillar of one of the world’s largest entertainment conglomerates.

Creatively, Lucasfilm might have taken greater formal risks. George Lucas historically prioritized technological innovation and experimental storytelling over market expectations. A non-Disney Lucasfilm could have invested further in digital production technologies or niche storytelling experiments, perhaps through the Skywalker Ranch Foundation or educational and artistic initiatives. However, financial risk tolerance would be lower without Disney’s capital reserves, limiting blockbuster-scale projects.

Culturally, fan polarization might look different. The Disney era triggered debates over canon resets, legacy character treatment, and corporate storytelling. Under Lucas, controversies would still exist—given reactions to the prequels—but they would stem from auteur decisions rather than corporate franchise management. The brand might feel more singular, for better or worse.

Finally, Disney itself would be in a weaker franchise position without *Star Wars*. The acquisition strengthened Disney’s dominance alongside Marvel and Pixar. Without it, streaming competition and franchise diversification strategies might have evolved differently.

In summary, if Lucasfilm had never been sold, *Star Wars* would likely be smaller in scale, slower in output, more centralized in creative control, and potentially more experimental—but less globally ubiquitous. The franchise might feel more cohesive and auteur-driven, yet less commercially expansive and culturally omnipresent.

items.question: What If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions?
human_answers: I don't think you understand SpaceX very well. The Starship "failures" are the result of rapid design-test-redesign, pushing the hardware to its limits to find out just what those limits actually are. I think they are up to the third generation design. If putting a Starship into orbit was so important to them, they'd have done by now. Still in test phase. Falcon 9 (and Heavy) is not about putting maximum mass into space, it is about putting payloads into space at minimum cost. So yes, a single type of engine and propellant all the way to orbit: the upper stage is just a cut-down version of the launcher and Merlin Vacuum is a Merlin 1D with a longer nozzle for more efficiency. Reusing a booster cuts payload mass by about 40%, but they break-even on the second or third flight. Falcon 9 is so cost-efficient that SpaceX is eating everyone else's lunch at this point. It's no Saturn V, to be sure, but it isn't meant to be. Saturn V was designed with each stage optimized just for its specific part of the mission... which made it extremely expensive to develop and build and totally uneconomic. A diametrically opposite design approach.

I actually like the idea of an improved dragon better than what we have with Starship (assuming it ever carries humans). As for using it for lunar missions. Do we need to recreate the Apollo Mission profile or can we build some sort of transfer craft a sort of tug or booster that can be docked with and used to get to and from the moon. We would need a way to refuel it in earth orbit but it may be one way to get Dragon to the moon. And long term it may be better. I have always thought that we needed some sort of “space craft” vs the way we do everything with the vehicle we use to get up and down from earth. That would I suppose be a big task to build and maintain and refuel this transfer vehicle. But it may allow a less powerful system to do the job. And once you have the hardware it is harder to cancel the thing. So we may actually get some long term use.

All true of course, also fully ignored in most cases and specifically in the articles/videos I cited above The "mantra" is simply that Dragon is cheaper and therefor better than Orion. Similar statements about Falcon versus SLS. One of the videos I didn't cite was in fact one that suggests Lunar HLS "Starship" will be used for ferrying the landing party from LEO to LLO where they would use Dragon to land on the Moon and then return to the HLS "Starship" to be ferried back to LEO where Dragon would be used to land on Earth. Ya, IIRC you lose the core stage. Ya it would be 'neat' but keep in mind the Super Draco's are not actually "throttleable" since they are supposed to be used as abort rockets and not landing rockets. The way the propellants are stored at very high pressures in order to get that high thrust for abort and I think that precludes landing use so they likely would have to be redesigned.. Randy
items.original_question: What if Falcon/Dragon to the Moon? Kind of bouncing off this thread as I've run across some of the usual "hype" sources such as this and this , (nothing from SpaceX though which I think is telling) "bragging" about SpaceX's "great new plan" to send crew Dragon to the Moon "sooner than NASA or China" etc, et-al. (Of course they all simply ignore the issues with Dragon going beyond LEO and the fact Orion and SLS are designed to do exactly that but what would I expect ) So the question is essentially "What if SpaceX had continued to iterate and improve Dragon and Falcon Heavy for use in Lunar missions? Granting that as I pointed out here that there's likely no "place" for such a move since the SpaceX to Mars focus was pretty much baked in since the start and with such a short timeline getting a plausible POD is going to be problematic I do wonder if a bit more focus on "Dear Moon" along with Cargo/Crew Dragon couldn't set up a premise where the eventual "HLS" might end up more realistic? Anyway, open for thoughts and comments Randy
