items.model_answer:
There isn’t a single exact amount, because it depends on the plumbing, water flow, and whether the cornstarch is dispersed or dumped in all at once. But the short answer is: even relatively small amounts can cause problems if they’re concentrated enough.

Cornstarch behaves very differently from many other kitchen substances. When dry, it’s a fine powder. When mixed with water, it forms a non-Newtonian fluid (like the classic “oobleck” experiment). At certain concentrations, it thickens dramatically under stress and can become paste-like or even temporarily solid. Inside a drain, that’s bad news.

If you pour a tablespoon or two of cornstarch down the drain with plenty of running water, it will likely disperse and wash through without major issues. Wastewater systems are designed to handle starches from food.

However, if you pour a large quantity—say a cup or more—especially if it mixes with only a small amount of water, it can form a thick slurry in the trap (the curved section under the sink) or farther down the pipe. That slurry can:

- Settle and partially block flow  
- Stick to pipe walls  
- Combine with grease or debris to form a more solid clog  

If left sitting, it can dry into a hard, glue-like residue that’s difficult to flush out. In narrow household plumbing (1.5–2 inch diameter pipes), it doesn’t take much buildup to significantly restrict flow.

So practically speaking, “bad things” can start happening with quantities on the order of a cup or more poured at once without sufficient water. Repeated smaller amounts over time can also accumulate and contribute to clogs.

The safe rule is simple: avoid disposing of significant amounts of dry cornstarch down the drain. If you need to discard a lot of it, put it in the trash instead.

If a stereo flew past you at twice the speed of sound (Mach 2), you would not hear it approaching in the normal way. Sound travels through air at about 343 m/s (around 1,235 km/h at sea level), so if the stereo were moving faster than that, it would outrun the sound waves it produces.

As it moves, the stereo would continuously emit sound—music, for example—but those sound waves would lag behind it. Because the source is moving faster than the waves can spread forward, the waves pile up into a shock front, forming what’s called a Mach cone. This is the same principle behind a sonic boom produced by supersonic aircraft.

To you, standing still, the stereo would appear to pass silently at first. You wouldn’t hear the music gradually getting louder as it approaches. Instead, after it has already passed you, the compressed shock wave would hit your ears as a sudden, sharp “boom.” Immediately after that, you would hear the music trailing behind it, distorted and rapidly fading as the source moves farther away.

The sound quality would be heavily altered. The Doppler effect would still apply, but in an extreme way: right after the boom, the sound would be shifted to a much lower frequency (lower pitch) because the source is moving away at supersonic speed. The music would likely sound stretched, warped, and compressed in time due to the changing geometry of how the sound waves reach you.

In short, you wouldn’t hear it coming—you’d experience a sonic boom first, and only then hear the distorted, receding music trailing behind the supersonic stereo.

items.question: What If We Launched a One-Way Mission to Voyager 1 Today?
human_answers: Voyager I is farther from Earth than any other manmade object. After getting a pair of gravitational kicks from Jupiter and Saturn, it’s headed out of the Solar System at a pretty high speed, and nothing else we’ve built is on track to pass it.

items.model_answer:
Voyager 1 is currently about 24–25 billion kilometers from Earth (roughly 160+ astronomical units) and moving away at about 17 km/s relative to the Sun. A one-way mission launched today to catch up with it would face extreme technical and physical challenges.

First, speed is the dominant issue. Voyager 1 itself was launched on a powerful Saturn V–class rocket and gained additional speed through gravity assists from Jupiter and Saturn. Even so, it took nearly 50 years to reach its current distance. To catch it in a reasonable time—say a few decades—a new spacecraft would need to travel significantly faster than Voyager 1. If we launched something that traveled only slightly faster, it might take many decades just to close the gap, because Voyager keeps moving away every second.

With current chemical rocket technology, matching and exceeding Voyager’s heliocentric speed is possible in principle but difficult without gravity assists. Using advanced propulsion—such as nuclear thermal rockets, nuclear electric propulsion, or a powerful solar Oberth maneuver close to the Sun—would improve the odds. Concepts like solar sails or laser-driven light sails could potentially reach much higher speeds, but those technologies are not yet operational at the required scale.

Second, navigation and communication would be demanding. At Voyager’s distance, radio signals take over 22 hours one way. Any rendezvous mission would require extremely precise trajectory planning over decades. Power generation would also be a constraint: solar panels are useless that far from the Sun, so the spacecraft would need a long-lived nuclear power source like a radioisotope thermoelectric generator or possibly a small fission reactor.

Third, actually “meeting” Voyager 1 would be delicate. Voyager is tiny on astronomical scales and not designed for docking. A flyby would be more realistic than a docking attempt. Even matching velocity closely would require careful fuel budgeting after decades of flight.

If successfully launched with advanced propulsion, a rendezvous might take 20–40 years in an optimistic scenario. With near-current technology, it could take half a century or more. The mission would be expensive and scientifically limited, since Voyager’s instruments are already outdated and failing. However, it could serve symbolic, engineering, or archival purposes—for example, inspecting Voyager, relaying data, or even attaching a new power or communication module (though that would be extremely complex).

In summary, a one-way mission to Voyager 1 is physically possible but technologically demanding and slow. It would require either major propulsion advances or acceptance of a multi-decade chase. The main barriers are speed, power, and the sheer scale of interstellar space—not any fundamental law of physics.

items.model_answer:
If everyone in America tried to drive west at the same time, the result would be immediate and overwhelming infrastructure collapse rather than any meaningful westward migration.

The U.S. has over 330 million people and more than 275 million registered vehicles. Highways are not designed to handle anywhere near that number of simultaneous travelers. Within minutes, major roads would gridlock. On-ramps, intersections, and city streets would become impassable. Emergency vehicles would be unable to move. Fuel supplies would be exhausted quickly because gas stations rely on continuous deliveries that require functioning roads. Once vehicles ran out of fuel, they would remain stranded, further blocking traffic.

Urban areas would become immobilized first, but rural highways would also jam rapidly as traffic bottlenecked toward major westbound routes. Critical services—food distribution, healthcare, power plant staffing—would fail because workers and supply chains would be trapped in traffic. Within days, shortages of food, water, and medical care would develop nationwide.

If people somehow continued pushing west over time, the western states—especially California, Oregon, and Washington—would face extreme overcrowding. Cities near the Pacific Ocean would have nowhere further west to expand, creating massive humanitarian and logistical crises. Coastal areas would become the final bottleneck, with millions unable to proceed any farther.

Environmentally, the event would cause enormous fuel consumption, air pollution, and likely thousands of accidents. Economically, the sudden halt of nearly all productive activity would trigger immediate collapse of markets and supply systems.

In short, instead of America shifting westward, the country would experience nationwide gridlock, infrastructure failure, economic shutdown, and humanitarian crisis within a very short time.

items.model_answer:
If a high-speed train had to go through a vertical loop, the main physical requirement would be that it maintain enough speed at the top of the loop to keep the train pressed against the track. At the very top, gravity pulls the train downward, and the track must supply enough inward (centripetal) force to keep it moving in a circle rather than falling. The minimum condition is that the centripetal acceleration equals gravitational acceleration, meaning \( v^2 / r \ge g \). So the minimum speed at the top is \( v = \sqrt{gr} \), where \( r \) is the loop’s radius.

In practice, the train would need to go significantly faster than this minimum to ensure safety and maintain contact under real-world conditions. That implies very high speeds for a large-radius loop, because high-speed trains are long and cannot handle tight curves. For example, if the loop radius were 500 meters (already extremely tight for a high-speed train), the minimum speed at the top would be about 70 m/s (around 250 km/h). To safely enter and exit the loop, the train would need even higher speed at the bottom to account for energy loss climbing upward.

The g-forces on passengers would also be a major issue. At the bottom of the loop, they would feel much heavier than normal because both gravity and the centripetal acceleration point upward relative to them. If the train barely met the minimum speed at the top (so passengers briefly feel weightless there), the force at the bottom would be about 3 g. Sustained 3 g forces are uncomfortable and potentially dangerous for unrestrained passengers, especially in a conventional train environment where people are standing or moving around.

Structurally, trains are not designed for such loads. High-speed trains rely on wheel-rail contact optimized for relatively gentle curves and small vertical accelerations. The mechanical stresses on wheels, axles, suspension, couplings between cars, and the track itself would be enormous in a loop. Keeping the train firmly attached to the rails might require a fully enclosed track or roller-coaster-style wheel assemblies that grip from multiple directions, which current rail systems do not use.

In short, while physics does not forbid a high-speed train from going through a vertical loop, it would require extreme speeds, impose large and uncomfortable g-forces, and demand completely different vehicle and track designs. In practical engineering terms, it would be far more like a giant roller coaster than a conventional high-speed rail system.

items.model_answer:
If you enlarged a typical bowling ball to the size of Earth, what happens depends entirely on whether you are only scaling up its size or also scaling up its mass and internal structure.

A standard bowling ball has a mass of about 7 kg and a diameter of about 22 cm. If you simply scaled its size up to Earth’s diameter (about 12,742 km) while keeping the same material density, its volume would increase enormously. Volume scales with the cube of the radius, so increasing the diameter by roughly 58 million times would increase the volume—and therefore the mass—by about (5.8 × 10⁷)³, which is roughly 2 × 10²³ times greater. That would give the enlarged bowling ball a mass on the order of 10²⁴ kg, comparable to Earth’s mass (about 6 × 10²⁴ kg), assuming similar density.

However, a real bowling ball is made of relatively low-density materials like polyester or urethane, with densities around 1.2 g/cm³. Earth’s average density is about 5.5 g/cm³ because it contains a massive iron-nickel core compressed by gravity. An Earth-sized bowling ball made of bowling ball material would therefore be significantly less massive than Earth—roughly one quarter of Earth’s mass. Its surface gravity would be proportionally weaker, perhaps around 2–3 m/s² instead of Earth’s 9.8 m/s². You would weigh much less standing on it.

But there’s a deeper issue: at Earth size, gravity would strongly compress the material. A bowling ball’s internal structure is not designed to withstand planet-scale pressures. Under its own gravity, the material would be squeezed, likely heating up and potentially changing phase. It might partially melt and differentiate, with denser components sinking inward. Over time, it would stop being a “bowling ball” in any meaningful structural sense and instead become a roughly spherical, self-gravitating body—more like a small, low-density planet.

So an Earth-sized bowling ball would not behave like a giant recreational object. It would become a planet-sized world with weaker gravity than Earth, possible internal melting due to compression, and a structure reshaped entirely by its own gravity.

items.model_answer:
What an alien civilization would see when looking at us depends almost entirely on how far away they are, because they would see Earth as it was in the past. Light takes time to travel.

If they live on the nearest potentially habitable exoplanet, such as Proxima Centauri b about 4.2 light‑years away, they would see Earth as it was 4.2 years ago. With technology comparable to or more advanced than ours, they would not see individual people or cities directly. Instead, they would likely detect:

- A small blue planet orbiting a G-type star.
- Strong atmospheric biosignatures such as oxygen, ozone, methane, and water vapor.
- Seasonal changes in vegetation reflected in subtle color shifts.
- Night-side artificial illumination, if their telescopes are extremely advanced.
- Radio and television leakage, which has been spreading outward from Earth for about 100 years in a roughly 100-light-year sphere.

If they are 50 light-years away, they would see Earth as it was 50 years ago—around the 1970s. If they are 100 light-years away, they would see early 20th-century Earth. At 65 million light-years away, they would see dinosaurs, not humans.

From a technological standpoint, our strongest detectable signatures are likely:

- Atmospheric oxygen in large quantities, which strongly suggests life.
- Industrial pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide or possibly chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), which could signal technological activity.
- Artificial radio emissions, which are detectable only within a limited distance unless deliberately powerful.

However, resolving surface features like continents, cities, or spacecraft would require extraordinary telescopes far larger than anything we currently possess. Even a very advanced civilization might see Earth as a pale, pixel-sized world with changing spectra rather than a detailed image.

In short, an alien civilization on the nearest habitable exoplanet would see a living planet with a technological species—just slightly in the past. The farther away they are, the deeper into Earth’s history they would be looking.

If they live on the nearest potentially habitable exoplanet, such as Proxima Centauri b about 4.2 light‑years away, they would see Earth as it was 4.2 years ago.
With technology comparable to or more advanced than ours, they would not see individual people or cities directly.
Instead, they would likely detect:
- A small blue planet orbiting a G-type star.
- Strong atmospheric biosignatures such as oxygen, ozone, methane, and water vapor.
- Seasonal changes in vegetation reflected in subtle color shifts.

criterion_evaluations.name: Light-travel-time and observational geometry fidelity
criterion_evaluations.reason: The answer accurately identifies Proxima Centauri b as the nearest potentially habitable exoplanet and correctly applies the ~4.2 light-year distance as a ~4.2-year observational delay. It consistently explains that more distant observers see earlier epochs and ties this to examples such as 50, 100, and 65 million light-years. It also incorporates observational limits, noting that aliens would likely infer Earth via spectra, biosignatures, radio leakage, and perhaps artificial illumination rather than directly seeing people or cities. However, it does not deeply address line-of-sight geometry, angular separation from the Sun, orbital viewing constraints, or how those constraints affect detectability, and some claims such as seeing a 'technological species' are somewhat stronger than the stated observational evidence supports. Strong satisfaction of the criterion, but not precise or expert-level enough for 9-10.

items.question: What If the Sun Suddenly Went Out?
human_answers: This is probably the single most popular question submitted to What If. Part of why I haven’t answered it is that it's been answered already.
items.original_question: 如果太阳突然熄灭，地球会发生什么？

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Sun Suddenly Went Out?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise handling for the Sun going dark
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer clearly defines and consistently reasons from the premise that the Sun suddenly stops emitting light/heat, while distinguishing this from the Sun physically disappearing or losing mass.
criteria.1-2: Confuses the premise, e.g. treats the Sun as exploding, vanishing, or Earth instantly freezing without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions the Sun going dark but mixes incompatible assumptions about light, heat, gravity, or mass.
criteria.5-6: Mostly assumes the Sun stops shining, but leaves key premise details ambiguous or occasionally inconsistent.
criteria.7-8: Clearly treats the Sun as no longer emitting radiation and mostly preserves gravity/orbits unless explicitly caveated.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames alternative interpretations, selects one, and keeps all downstream reasoning consistent with that premise.

criteria.name: Immediate physical consequences and timescales
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of near-term effects after the Sun goes out, including the roughly 8-minute light-travel delay, loss of daylight, temperature decline, and radiation changes.
criteria.1-2: Gives implausible instant effects with no timescale awareness.
criteria.3-4: Includes darkness or cold but misses the 8-minute delay and gives vague or incorrect timing.
criteria.5-6: Notes some correct immediate effects, but timing and mechanisms are incomplete or partially wrong.
criteria.7-8: Accurately covers the 8-minute delay, rapid darkness, and progressive cooling with reasonable timescales.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent sequence from first minutes to days/weeks, with accurate physical mechanisms and no exaggeration.

criteria.name: Earth climate, oceans, atmosphere, and habitability chain
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the depth and plausibility of downstream Earth-system reasoning: surface cooling, weather collapse, freezing oceans, atmospheric changes, and possible refuges.
criteria.1-2: Claims all life or oceans vanish immediately, or gives fantasy outcomes unsupported by physics.
criteria.3-4: Mentions freezing and death but lacks mechanisms, order, or realistic staging.
criteria.5-6: Covers major effects such as cooling, photosynthesis failure, and ocean freezing, but shallowly or with rough errors.
criteria.7-8: Explains staged collapse of climate, food webs, surface habitability, and oceans with plausible timing.
criteria.9-10: Integrates climate inertia, ocean heat capacity, geothermal heat, atmosphere behavior, and survival niches into a realistic long-range chain.

criteria.name: Biological and human civilization consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces effects on ecosystems, agriculture, energy systems, infrastructure, and potential human survival strategies under prolonged solar absence.
criteria.1-2: Only states that everyone dies or gives unsupported survival claims.
criteria.3-4: Mentions plant death or human hardship but omits food, energy, and ecological cascades.
criteria.5-6: Identifies photosynthesis collapse, food-chain failure, and human shelter needs, but with limited causal depth.
criteria.7-8: Connects ecosystem collapse to agriculture, power, heating, logistics, and underground/technological refuges.
criteria.9-10: Offers a nuanced survival analysis including stored food, artificial light, nuclear/geothermal power, deep ocean vents, and long-term limits.

criteria.name: Long-range coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a coherent causal timeline from minutes to years or longer, appropriately signals uncertainty, and avoids internal contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Is internally contradictory, temporally chaotic, or confidently asserts impossible outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Has a loose sequence but frequent contradictions or unjustified certainty.
criteria.5-6: Presents a generally plausible timeline but with gaps, overconfident claims, or minor inconsistencies.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear causal progression and flags uncertain estimates or premise-dependent outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a robust long-range scenario with calibrated uncertainty, explicit assumptions, and no meaningful contradictions.

items.model_answer:
If the Sun suddenly went out—meaning it instantly stopped emitting light and heat—the effects would unfold in stages.

First, nothing would change immediately. Because light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to Earth, we would continue seeing and feeling sunlight for that long. After that delay, the sky would go completely dark (except for stars and artificial light), and Earth would begin cooling rapidly.

Within hours, surface temperatures would start dropping significantly. Photosynthesis would stop immediately once sunlight vanished, so plants would no longer produce energy. Within a few days, average global temperatures would fall below freezing. Within about a week, Earth’s average surface temperature could drop to around –17°C (1°F), and it would continue falling over time.

After a year, the average surface temperature could reach roughly –73°C (–100°F). Oceans would begin freezing from the top down, but they would not freeze solid quickly. Water retains heat well, so the deeper ocean layers could remain liquid for a long time, insulated by thick surface ice.

Most surface life would die within weeks to months. Plants would die first, then herbivores, then carnivores. Humans could survive temporarily using artificial heat, nuclear power, and geothermal energy. Long-term survival would likely depend on living underground or near geothermal or nuclear energy sources, possibly near deep-sea hydrothermal vents.

Gravitationally, if the Sun only stopped shining but retained its mass, Earth would continue orbiting normally in darkness. However, if the Sun somehow vanished entirely (including its mass), Earth would stop orbiting and move in a straight line into space at its current orbital speed.

In summary, the sudden loss of the Sun would quickly plunge Earth into darkness and extreme cold, collapse most ecosystems within weeks to months, and leave only technologically or geothermally supported life able to survive for any extended period.

items.model_answer:
Rowing across a “lake” depends mostly on the liquid’s density, viscosity, temperature, and chemical reactivity. These six substances differ so dramatically that the experience would range from merely strange to instantly fatal.

A lake of **mercury** would be the most physically plausible to row on. Mercury is about 13.5 times denser than water, so a boat would float extremely high, almost like sitting on a heavy metal cushion. The oars would feel unusual: mercury is about 1.5 times more viscous than water, so each stroke would feel thicker and heavier but still manageable. However, mercury is toxic and produces harmful vapor, so without serious protection you’d be poisoned by inhalation. Mechanically possible; biologically dangerous.

A lake of **bromine** would be far worse. Bromine is a dense, reddish-brown liquid, about three times denser than water, and it releases highly corrosive, toxic fumes. It would attack your skin, eyes, lungs, and most materials. Even if you had a boat that could float (which it could, since bromine is denser than water), you would be rapidly chemically burned and poisoned. The fumes alone would likely be fatal. Rowing wouldn’t last long.

A lake of **gallium** would be surreal but survivable in principle. Gallium melts at about 30 °C, so on a warm day it could be liquid. It’s dense (about six times denser than water) but only moderately viscous. A boat would float very high. Gallium is not highly toxic, but it wets and weakens many metals, especially aluminum, causing structural failure. If your boat or oars contained aluminum, they could crumble. The liquid would feel heavy and metallic, and splashes would look like flowing silver. It would be strange but not immediately deadly.

A lake of **tungsten** is essentially impossible under normal planetary conditions. Tungsten melts at over 3400 °C. At that temperature, everything around would glow white-hot. The radiant heat alone would vaporize you and any conventional boat long before you got near it. Even if some exotic materials let you approach, the liquid would be extremely dense (about 19 times denser than water), so a boat would float extremely high. But in practice, the environment would resemble a stellar furnace.

A lake of **liquid nitrogen** would be lethally cold. At −196 °C, it would instantly freeze living tissue on contact. The surface would boil violently wherever it touched anything warmer, surrounding your boat with clouds of fog. A boat could float—liquid nitrogen is less dense than water, but still dense enough to support typical materials. The main sensation would be intense cold, cracking materials, and constant boiling. You would need extreme insulation and oxygen, since nitrogen vapor would displace breathable air.

A lake of **liquid helium** would be even stranger. At around −269 °C, it’s near absolute zero. Liquid helium has extremely low density and almost no viscosity. In its superfluid state (below 2.17 K), it flows without friction, creeps up walls, and leaks through microscopic cracks. Rowing would feel almost impossible because the oars would experience very little drag—there’s hardly anything to “push” against. Your strokes would generate minimal propulsion. Meanwhile, the cold would instantly freeze unprotected materials and flesh, and the liquid would boil explosively on contact with anything warmer. It would feel less like rowing through a fluid and more like sitting in a ghostly, nearly frictionless cryogenic mist.

In summary, mercury and gallium would be physically rowable but hazardous in different ways; bromine would chemically destroy you; liquid nitrogen and helium would freeze you instantly (with helium behaving in bizarre, almost frictionless ways); and liquid tungsten would exist only in an inferno where neither you nor your boat could survive.

items.model_answer:
If you dropped 3,000 Super Balls (the small, highly elastic rubber balls) from a seven‑story parking garage onto a pedestrian, the outcome would depend on several physical factors: the height, the mass of each ball, their bounciness, how tightly they’re clustered, and whether they hit all at once or spread out.

Let’s estimate the physics.

A seven‑story garage is roughly 20–25 meters tall. An object dropped from 25 meters hits the ground at about 22 m/s (around 50 mph), ignoring air resistance. A typical Super Ball weighs about 10 grams (0.01 kg). The kinetic energy of one ball at impact would be:

KE = ½mv² ≈ ½ × 0.01 × (22²) ≈ 2.4 joules.

That’s roughly the energy of being hit by a hard-thrown small pebble. Painful, possibly leaving a welt, but unlikely to cause serious injury by itself.

Now multiply by 3,000 balls:

Total mass = 30 kg (about 66 pounds).
Total kinetic energy ≈ 7,200 joules.

That sounds large — comparable to the energy of a handgun bullet — but there’s a key difference: the energy is distributed across thousands of separate small impacts, not concentrated in one projectile.

Because Super Balls are extremely elastic, most of their energy goes into bouncing back up rather than transferring fully into the person. They would strike, compress briefly, and rebound, reducing how much force is delivered compared to something that sticks or shatters.

So what would happen in reality?

If they were released in a tight cluster and hit someone directly on the head or shoulders, the person would likely experience:

- Numerous painful impacts
- Bruising and welts
- Possible cuts around the face or scalp
- Risk of concussion if several balls strike the head simultaneously
- Loss of balance, possibly leading to a fall

However, it is unlikely to be fatal under normal conditions. The individual balls are too light to penetrate or cause deep blunt trauma. The bigger danger might come from secondary effects — slipping on bouncing balls, falling backward, or being struck in the eye.

There’s also a strong chaotic effect: Super Balls bounce unpredictably. Many would ricochet away midair after hitting others, so not all 3,000 would hit the person. The scene would be noisy and chaotic, with balls rebounding in all directions.

In short: extremely painful and potentially injurious, especially to the head or eyes, but probably not lethal. The most serious risks would come from loss of balance or unlucky clustered impacts rather than the raw energy of the balls themselves.

items.model_answer:
Assume a circular hole 10 meters in diameter is opened at Challenger Deep (about 11,000 m below sea level) and that it somehow leads to empty space or an infinite void so the water can freely escape. We’ll also assume the hole stays open and does not collapse under crustal pressure.

The flow rate would be limited by how fast water can accelerate through a 10‑meter opening under the pressure of the overlying ocean. Using Torricelli’s law, the exit speed of water under a depth \( h \) is approximately:

v ≈ √(2gh)

For a typical ocean depth of about 4,000 m (the global average), this gives:

v ≈ √(2 × 9.8 × 4000) ≈ 280 m/s.

A 10‑meter diameter hole has a radius of 5 m, so its area is:

A ≈ πr² ≈ 78.5 m².

The initial maximum flow rate would therefore be roughly:

Q ≈ A × v ≈ 78.5 × 280 ≈ 22,000 m³/s.

Earth’s oceans contain about 1.3 × 10¹⁸ m³ of water. Dividing total volume by this flow rate:

Time ≈ (1.3 × 10¹⁸ m³) / (2.2 × 10⁴ m³/s)  
≈ 6 × 10¹³ seconds  
≈ about 2 million years.

That’s an optimistic lower bound. As the ocean level drops, the pressure head decreases, so the flow rate slows continuously. The final draining would take significantly longer than the initial estimate. Realistically, it would take several million years.

Long before the oceans fully drained, the consequences would be catastrophic. Sea levels would steadily fall, exposing continental shelves, altering coastlines, and collapsing marine ecosystems. Climate systems would destabilize as evaporation and heat transport patterns changed. Atmospheric composition would shift as marine life died off. Eventually, most complex life on Earth would be wiped out.

In short, even with a 10‑meter-wide hole at the deepest point, the oceans would not vanish quickly. It would take millions of years, but the biosphere would be devastated long before the last water disappeared.

items.model_answer:
If you could somehow teleport all of Earth’s oceans onto Mars, the planet would change dramatically—but not into a second Earth.

First, the scale: Earth’s oceans contain about 1.4 billion cubic kilometers of water. If spread evenly over Mars, whose surface area is about 28% of Earth’s, that would create a global ocean roughly 2–3 kilometers deep. Mars would become a true water world.

Initially, the water would behave violently. Mars’ average surface temperature is about −60 °C, and its atmospheric pressure is less than 1% of Earth’s. At such low pressure, liquid water is unstable: it either freezes or boils. So when the oceans arrived, much of the water would begin boiling vigorously, even at cold temperatures, while other portions would rapidly freeze. You’d get a chaotic mix of steam-filled skies, vast ice formation, and turbulent supercooled liquid water.

The water vapor released into the atmosphere would thicken it substantially. Mars’ gravity (about 38% of Earth’s) is strong enough to hold water vapor, so a much denser, steam-rich atmosphere would form. This would create a strong greenhouse effect, raising surface temperatures. As the planet warmed, more liquid water could remain stable at the surface, at least temporarily.

However, there are major long-term problems. Mars lacks a global magnetic field, so over time the solar wind would strip away water vapor from the upper atmosphere. Ultraviolet sunlight would split water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen; the lightweight hydrogen would escape to space, and much of the oxygen would either escape or react with surface rocks (oxidizing them further). This process would gradually dry the planet again over millions to hundreds of millions of years.

Additionally, some of the water would freeze permanently at the poles or as subsurface ice, because Mars is farther from the Sun and receives only about 43% of the sunlight Earth does. Even with a thicker atmosphere, maintaining warm, Earth-like oceans would be difficult without additional greenhouse gases.

In the short term (thousands to millions of years), Mars might experience a warm, wet phase with oceans, rainfall, rivers, and an active water cycle. In the long term, unless you also gave Mars a thicker, more stable atmosphere and magnetic protection, much of that water would either freeze or slowly be lost to space.

So dumping Earth’s oceans onto Mars would temporarily transform it into a blue, ocean-covered world—but it would not permanently turn Mars into a second Earth.

items.model_answer:
If you tried to hold an airplane to the ground with a rope while it was attempting to take off, whether you’d succeed depends entirely on the forces involved.

An airplane takes off when its engines generate enough thrust to overcome drag and rolling resistance and accelerate to a speed where the wings produce sufficient lift. The engines can produce enormous force. For example, a small single-engine propeller plane might generate a few thousand newtons of thrust, while a large commercial jet engine can produce over 100,000 newtons of thrust per engine.

If you tied a rope from the airplane to the ground and tried to hold it by hand, you would lose instantly. The force produced by even a small aircraft engine far exceeds what a human can resist. The rope would either yank you forward violently or rip out of your hands. If you somehow anchored yourself firmly, you would likely be injured before you could stop the plane.

If instead the rope were tied to a solid anchor point—like a massive concrete block or a heavy vehicle—the outcome would depend on the strength of the rope and the anchor. If the anchor and rope could withstand more force than the airplane’s engines produce, the airplane would not move forward. The engines would still be running at full thrust, but the plane would remain stationary, similar to how aircraft are secured during engine tests. If the rope or anchor were weaker than the engine thrust, they would fail—either snapping or being dragged.

In short, you personally could not hold an airplane down with a rope. Only a sufficiently strong anchor and rope could counteract the engine’s thrust. The physics is simply a balance of forces: if the restraining force exceeds the engine thrust, the plane stays put; if not, it moves.

items.question: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?
human_answers: The one-inch gap would take about 70 milliseconds to close. Don't stick your hand in.
items.original_question: 如果一座巨大的山峰（比如麦金利山）的底部一英寸消失了怎么办？山体下降1英寸的影响会发生什么？ 1英尺呢？如果山脚升高到山顶现在的高度，然后让整个山落到地上怎么办？

criteria.name: Initial mechanical response and gap-closure timing
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons from the premise that the bottom inch of a massive mountain vanishes to the immediate gravitational drop, including the approximate timescale for the one-inch gap to close.
criteria.1-2: Claims the mountain floats, explodes instantly, or otherwise ignores gravity and gap closure.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes downward motion but gives an implausible or unsupported timescale.
criteria.5-6: Identifies rapid collapse of the one-inch gap but lacks quantitative reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Gives a plausible free-fall estimate near 70 ms with minor caveats or omissions.
criteria.9-10: Correctly explains free-fall closure of one inch in about 70 ms and notes the extreme danger of anything in the gap.

criteria.name: Causal fidelity to the counterfactual premise
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer stays faithful to the exact scenario: only the bottom inch vanishes beneath a massive mountain, rather than changing the amount, location, or physical assumptions without justification.
criteria.1-2: Replaces the premise with a different event, such as the whole mountain disappearing or levitating.
criteria.3-4: Frequently drifts from the one-inch removal premise or invents unsupported conditions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly keeps the premise but occasionally exaggerates or alters the geometry.
criteria.7-8: Maintains the one-inch basal void premise and reasons from it consistently.
criteria.9-10: Strictly preserves the premise while explicitly handling idealizations such as support, terrain contact, and material continuity.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage of stress, impact, and deformation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the physical mechanisms following gap closure, including impact, compression waves, fracturing, landslides, and redistribution of stresses through the mountain.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only a vague collapse with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions impact or shaking but omits stress propagation and deformation.
criteria.5-6: Covers impact and some cracking or settling, but mechanisms are shallow.
criteria.7-8: Explains impact, stress waves, fracture, local crushing, and possible slope failures.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent multi-mechanism account including free fall, impact deceleration, seismic waves, rock failure, and uneven settling.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects and scale calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly extends the immediate event into later consequences without overstating global effects, considering local seismic shaking, dust, avalanches, infrastructure damage, and stabilization.
criteria.1-2: Predicts absurd global catastrophe or no aftermath at all.
criteria.3-4: Lists effects but with severe scale errors, such as planetwide destruction.
criteria.5-6: Mentions some local aftermath but lacks scale discipline or sequencing.
criteria.7-8: Plausibly describes local-to-regional shaking, rockfalls, dust, and damage over seconds to days.
criteria.9-10: Clearly sequences immediate closure, impact, seismic response, landslides, structural damage, aftershocks, and eventual settling with realistic scale limits.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes robust conclusions from assumptions, avoids internal contradictions, and handles unknowns such as mountain shape, rock strength, and contact conditions.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident contradictory claims or impossible statements.
criteria.3-4: Shows some uncertainty but contains major contradictions or unjustified certainty.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges unknowns but mixes firm and speculative claims inconsistently.

items.model_answer:
If the bottom inch of a massive mountain instantly vanished, the mountain would immediately lose the support that holds it up, and gravity would take over. Rock is strong under compression, but it cannot float unsupported. The entire mass above that missing layer would begin to fall.

What happens next depends on the mountain’s size and structure, but in general the result would be catastrophic collapse.

As the base disappears, the mountain would drop roughly one inch before slamming into the ground beneath it. That may sound small, but for a mountain weighing trillions of tons, even a one‑inch fall releases an enormous amount of energy. The energy released would be comparable to a very large earthquake. The sudden impact would generate intense seismic waves that could register as a major quake across a wide region.

The structure of the mountain would also likely fail. Rock is brittle under tension and shear. When the base vanishes, the lower portions would fracture almost instantly. The falling mass would not remain intact; it would shatter, triggering massive landslides and possibly a cascading collapse of large sections of the mountain. Nearby valleys could be buried under debris avalanches moving at high speed.

There would also be a strong air blast from the sudden displacement of air as the mountain drops and collapses. Dust clouds would be enormous, potentially rising kilometers into the atmosphere.

If the mountain were volcanic, the sudden unloading and impact might alter pressures in the magma chamber below, possibly triggering or accelerating an eruption.

Importantly, the Earth itself would not be seriously affected on a planetary scale. Mountains already press into the crust under their weight (a concept called isostasy), and the crust supports them. The event would be locally devastating, but it would not destabilize the planet.

In short, removing the bottom inch of a massive mountain would cause it to collapse violently, generate powerful earthquakes and landslides, and devastate the surrounding region—but Earth as a whole would remain intact.

items.model_answer:
If a spacecraft tried to use rockets to slow itself to just a few miles per hour during atmospheric reentry, it would be theoretically possible but practically unrealistic and extremely inefficient.

When a spacecraft returns to Earth from orbit, it is traveling about 17,500 mph (28,000 km/h). That speed corresponds to enormous kinetic energy. In normal reentry, the spacecraft does not use rockets to remove that energy. Instead, it allows atmospheric drag to convert the kinetic energy into heat, which is absorbed and shed by a heat shield. The atmosphere does the braking “for free,” at the cost of intense heating.

If you tried to use rockets to slow from orbital speed down to just a few mph before encountering significant atmosphere, you would essentially need to cancel nearly all of your orbital velocity. That would require a delta‑v almost equal to what was needed to reach orbit in the first place. In other words, you would need nearly as much propellant to slow down as you originally needed to launch. For most spacecraft, this would mean carrying several times their own mass in extra fuel—far beyond practical limits.

Even if you waited until entering the atmosphere and then tried to fire rockets continuously to maintain only a few mph, the engines would have to counteract both gravity and the vehicle’s remaining forward motion. To hover or descend at a few mph from high altitude, the thrust would need to roughly equal the spacecraft’s weight for an extended period, requiring enormous fuel reserves. The propellant mass required would be prohibitive for anything returning from orbit.

There are limited versions of this idea in practice. For example, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 booster uses rocket burns to significantly slow down before landing, and some lunar or Martian landers use rockets for soft landings. However, those vehicles are either suborbital, much smaller, or accept large fuel penalties. A full orbital spacecraft attempting to cancel nearly all its speed with rockets alone would be extremely heavy and inefficient.

So while physics does not forbid it, using rockets to slow to just a few miles per hour during Earth reentry would require impractically large amounts of fuel, making atmospheric drag by far the more efficient and practical method.

items.model_answer:
If you tried to print the entire English Wikipedia in real time, the result would be physically enormous and practically unmanageable—but not impossible in principle.

The English Wikipedia currently has roughly 6–7 million articles. If the average article contains about 600–700 words, that puts the total near 4–5 billion words. A typical printed page holds about 500 words, so you would need on the order of 8–10 million pages.

At a fast office printer speed of 30 pages per minute, printing 9 million pages would take:

9,000,000 ÷ 30 ≈ 300,000 minutes  
≈ 5,000 hours  
≈ 200 days of nonstop printing.

That’s over half a year of continuous operation, assuming no paper jams, no ink refills, and no downtime.

The physical stack would also be extreme. A single sheet of paper is about 0.1 millimeters thick. Ten million sheets would form a stack about 1,000 meters tall—roughly the height of three Eiffel Towers stacked vertically. At about 5 grams per sheet, the paper would weigh around 45–50 metric tons.

And that’s just for one snapshot in time.

Wikipedia is constantly edited—often several edits per minute across the site. If you meant printing it “in real time” as it updates, you’d never truly finish, because new content is always being added. You would either always be slightly behind or you would need to continuously reprint updated pages, generating an endless flow of paper.

So physically, you could print a snapshot of Wikipedia with enough time, paper, money, and industrial patience. But keeping up with it in real time would turn into a never-ending, warehouse-filling paper stream.

edus.text: If you tried to print the entire English Wikipedia in real time,
the result would be physically enormous and practically unmanageable
but not impossible in principle.
The English Wikipedia currently has roughly 6–7 million articles.
If the average article contains about 600–700 words,
that puts the total near 4–5 billion words.
A typical printed page holds about 500 words,
so you would need on the order of 8–10 million pages.
At a fast office printer speed of 30 pages per minute,
printing 9 million pages would take 9,000,000 ÷ 30 ≈ 300,000 minutes.
That is approximately 5,000 hours.
That is approximately 200 days of nonstop printing.
That’s over half a year of continuous operation,
assuming no paper jams, no ink refills, and no downtime.
The physical stack would also be extreme.
A single sheet of paper is about 0.1 millimeters thick.
Ten million sheets would form a stack about 1,000 meters tall.
That is roughly the height of three Eiffel Towers stacked vertically.
At about 5 grams per sheet,
the paper would weigh around 45–50 metric tons.
And that’s just for one snapshot in time.
Wikipedia is constantly edited.
It is often edited several times per minute across the site.
If you meant printing it “in real time” as it updates,
you’d never truly finish,
because new content is always being added.
You would either always be slightly behind
or you would need to continuously reprint updated pages,
generating an endless flow of paper.
So physically, you could print a snapshot of Wikipedia with enough time, paper, money, and industrial patience.
But keeping up with it in real time would turn into a never-ending, warehouse-filling paper stream.

items.model_answer:
If you jumped from a plane wearing helium tanks and deployed a giant balloon, whether you would float or fall depends entirely on buoyancy versus your total weight.

Helium provides lift because it is less dense than air. At sea level, one cubic meter of helium can lift about 1 kilogram (roughly 2.2 pounds), after subtracting the weight of the displaced air. So if you weigh 80 kg (about 176 pounds), you would need at least 80 cubic meters of helium just to hover—and more than that to overcome the weight of the balloon material, tanks, harness, and equipment. In practice, you might need 100 cubic meters or more. That’s an enormous balloon, roughly 5–6 meters in diameter (about 16–20 feet).

If the balloon were large enough and fully inflated before or immediately after the jump, it could slow your descent dramatically, potentially making you rise instead of fall. However, deploying such a large balloon mid-air would be extremely difficult. At high altitude, the air is less dense, so helium provides less lift. As you descend into denser air, the balloon would gain lifting power. Conversely, if you inflated it at high altitude, the helium would expand as pressure drops, risking rupture unless the balloon were designed for it.

There are also serious stability issues. A giant balloon attached above you would act like a pendulum. Air currents could cause spinning or violent oscillations. Without careful control surfaces or venting systems, you might not descend safely or predictably.

In short, if the balloon were large enough and properly engineered, you could float or descend very slowly instead of plummeting. But the balloon would have to be enormous, carefully managed for pressure changes, and structurally strong. Otherwise, you would simply fall—perhaps a bit slower, but not magically float away.

edus.text: If you jumped from a plane wearing helium tanks and deployed a giant balloon,
whether you would float or fall depends entirely on buoyancy versus your total weight.
Helium provides lift
because it is less dense than air.
At sea level, one cubic meter of helium can lift about 1 kilogram, roughly 2.2 pounds,
after subtracting the weight of the displaced air.
So if you weigh 80 kg, about 176 pounds,
you would need at least 80 cubic meters of helium just to hover
and more than that to overcome the weight of the balloon material, tanks, harness, and equipment.
In practice, you might need 100 cubic meters or more.
That’s an enormous balloon,
roughly 5–6 meters in diameter, about 16–20 feet.
If the balloon were large enough and fully inflated before or immediately after the jump,
it could slow your descent dramatically,
potentially making you rise instead of fall.
However, deploying such a large balloon mid-air would be extremely difficult.
At high altitude, the air is less dense,
so helium provides less lift.
As you descend into denser air,
the balloon would gain lifting power.
Conversely, if you inflated it at high altitude,
the helium would expand as pressure drops,
risking rupture
unless the balloon were designed for it.
There are also serious stability issues.
A giant balloon attached above you would act like a pendulum.
Air currents could cause spinning or violent oscillations.
Without careful control surfaces or venting systems,
you might not descend safely or predictably.
In short, if the balloon were large enough and properly engineered,
you could float or descend very slowly instead of plummeting.
But the balloon would have to be enormous, carefully managed for pressure changes, and structurally strong.
Otherwise, you would simply fall
perhaps a bit slower,
but not magically float away.

rubrics.question_focus: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise fidelity and scale recognition
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently accepts the premise that all digital data must be stored on physical punch cards and correctly reasons about the enormous scale of modern digital storage, especially relative to large organizations such as Google.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or rejects the punch-card premise, or treats punch cards as roughly equivalent to modern storage.
criteria.3-4: Mentions punch cards but severely underestimates the scale of global or organizational data storage.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that punch cards would be vastly larger and less efficient than modern storage, but gives only rough or incomplete scale reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains the extreme physical scale, storage density limits, and logistical burden implied by storing modern digital data on punch cards.
criteria.9-10: Provides highly coherent scale reasoning, including approximate comparisons, uncertainty about exact data volumes, and implications for entities like Google or global data centers.

items.model_answer:
If all digital data were stored on punch cards, modern society would slow down to a near standstill, limited by extreme physical, spatial, and mechanical constraints.

Punch cards store information as patterns of holes in stiff paper, typically representing one line of data per card. A standard 80-column punch card stores about 80 bytes. By contrast, a single modern smartphone photo might take up 3–5 megabytes—roughly 40,000 to 60,000 punch cards for just one image. A one-terabyte hard drive would require on the order of 12.5 trillion punch cards. Physically, that would fill enormous warehouses, likely covering many square kilometers and weighing millions of tons.

Storage would not only be massive but also slow. Accessing data would require physically locating and mechanically reading specific cards. Random access—instantly jumping to any file—would be nearly impossible. Instead, data retrieval would resemble searching through paper archives. Even with automated machinery, speeds would be constrained by the mechanics of feeding, sorting, and transporting physical cards. Internet-scale services like streaming, cloud computing, or real-time AI systems would be infeasible because the latency and throughput would be orders of magnitude too low.

Reliability would also suffer. Punch cards degrade, warp, tear, and burn. They are sensitive to moisture and mishandling. Large datasets would require constant physical maintenance and climate-controlled storage. Error rates would be much higher, and backups would multiply the already enormous space requirements.

Energy use would shift dramatically. Instead of energy-efficient solid-state storage, we would rely on mechanical readers, motors, and vast physical infrastructure. Transportation of data would involve physically moving stacks of cards rather than transmitting bits electronically, making global communication slow and resource-intensive.

Computing itself would be constrained. Programs stored on punch cards must be fed sequentially into machines. Interactive software, dynamic updates, and large-scale databases would be impractical. edus.text: If all digital data were stored on punch cards,
modern society would slow down to a near standstill, limited by extreme physical, spatial, and mechanical constraints.
Punch cards store information as patterns of holes in stiff paper,
typically representing one line of data per card.
A standard 80-column punch card stores about 80 bytes.
By contrast, a single modern smartphone photo might take up 3–5 megabytes—
roughly 40,000 to 60,000 punch cards for just one image.
A one-terabyte hard drive would require on the order of 12.5 trillion punch cards.
Physically, that would fill enormous warehouses, likely covering many square kilometers and weighing millions of tons.
Storage would not only be massive but also slow.
Accessing data would require physically locating and mechanically reading specific cards.
Random access—instantly jumping to any file—would be nearly impossible.
Instead, data retrieval would resemble searching through paper archives.
Even with automated machinery, speeds would be constrained by the mechanics of feeding, sorting, and transporting physical cards.
Internet-scale services like streaming, cloud computing, or real-time AI systems would be infeasible
because the latency and throughput would be orders of magnitude too low.
Reliability would also suffer.
Punch cards degrade, warp, tear, and burn.
They are sensitive to moisture and mishandling.
Large datasets would require constant physical maintenance and climate-controlled storage.
Error rates would be much higher,
and backups would multiply the already enormous space requirements.
Energy use would shift dramatically.
Instead of energy-efficient solid-state storage, we would rely on mechanical readers, motors, and vast physical infrastructure.
Transportation of data would involve physically moving stacks of cards
rather than transmitting bits electronically,
making global communication slow and resource-intensive.
Computing itself would be constrained.
Programs stored on punch cards must be fed sequentially into machines.
Interactive software, dynamic updates, and large-scale databases would be impractical.
Fields like machine learning, genomics, real-time financial markets, video streaming, and social media would either not exist or operate at extremely small scales.
In short, storing all digital data on punch cards would make today’s information age impossible.
Data would be scarce, slow, expensive, and overwhelmingly physical.
Modern computing depends fundamentally on dense, fast, electronic storage;
replacing it with punch cards would push us back to a mid-20th-century technological level,
unable to sustain contemporary digital society.

items.model_answer:
One foot per second is a very gentle speed—about 0.3 meters per second, or 0.68 miles per hour. But if you kept rising at that steady rate without ever stopping, the long-term consequences would be dramatic.

In the first few minutes, nothing unusual happens; you just drift upward like a very slow elevator. After an hour you’d be 3,600 feet high. After a full day, you’d be about 86,400 feet up—roughly 16 miles, well above commercial aircraft and into the stratosphere.

The commonly defined “edge of space” (the Kármán line at 100 km, or about 62 miles) is about 328,000 feet up. At one foot per second, you would reach that altitude in roughly 91 hours—just under four days. So in less than a week, you’d be in space.

After one year, you’d be about 31.5 million feet above Earth—around 6,000 miles (9,600 km). That’s higher than most satellites, but still well within Earth’s gravitational influence. Gravity weakens with height, but it never suddenly shuts off. You would not be in orbit, because orbit requires enormous sideways speed (about 17,500 mph near Earth), not just upward motion. Unless some force continuously pushed you upward at exactly 1 ft/s, you would simply fall back down. So this scenario assumes a constant upward force that keeps your speed steady.

If that upward motion continued indefinitely:

- In about 40 years, you would reach the Moon’s average distance (about 384,000 km).
- In about 16,000 years, you would travel one astronomical unit—the distance from Earth to the Sun.
- Given enough time, you would drift out of the solar system.

Although 1 ft/s is far below Earth’s escape velocity (about 11.2 km/s at the surface), escape velocity only applies if you’re coasting without propulsion. If a force keeps pushing you upward continuously, you can climb arbitrarily far, because that force keeps supplying the energy needed to work against gravity.

So the short-term result is that you’d reach space in days. The long-term result is that, given a sustained upward push and enough time, you would slowly drift past the Moon, through the solar system, and eventually into interstellar space—all at the pace of a brisk walking speed.

items.model_answer:
If wind reached 500 miles per hour (about 800 km/h), it would be far beyond the strength of even the most violent hurricanes and comparable to the strongest tornadoes ever recorded. At that speed, the wind would cause catastrophic and near-total destruction to most human-built structures.

For comparison, Category 5 hurricanes have sustained winds of about 157 mph or higher, and even that level can level buildings and uproot trees. The strongest tornadoes may briefly approach 300 mph. Five hundred mph would be in an entirely different class. The force exerted by wind increases with the square of its speed, so 500 mph winds would apply roughly ten times more pressure than 160 mph winds. Ordinary houses, high-rises, bridges, and most infrastructure would fail. Trees would be stripped and snapped, vehicles lifted or shredded, and debris would become lethal high-speed projectiles.

At 500 mph, the wind speed would be about two-thirds the speed of sound at sea level. Airflow around structures would create extreme aerodynamic forces, shock-like pressure effects, and intense turbulence. The environment would resemble conditions inside a powerful tornado vortex, but on whatever scale the wind field covered—if it extended over a large region, the devastation would be widespread and unprecedented.

Humans exposed directly would not survive due to impact with debris, inability to breathe properly in such violent airflow, and being thrown against objects. Even reinforced concrete buildings would be at serious risk depending on design.

In nature, sustained 500 mph winds do not occur in Earth’s weather systems under normal conditions. If they did, it would likely indicate an extreme and abnormal atmospheric event, such as a massively intensified storm system driven by unusual energy inputs.

In short, 500 mph wind would be overwhelmingly destructive, stripping landscapes, destroying most structures, and posing near-total danger to anything in its path.

items.question: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?
human_answers: Last week, we looked at at life on a giant world (http://what-if.xkcd.com/67/). This week, let's look at a small one.
items.original_question: 如果一颗小行星很小但质量却很大，你真的能像小王子一样住在上面吗？

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Physical Feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer defines a coherent tiny-but-ultra-massive asteroid scenario and respects constraints from density, radius, mass, and possible gravitational collapse.
criteria.1-2: Treats the asteroid like an ordinary rock or planet without addressing the tiny/high-mass premise.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges unusual mass or gravity but leaves the setup vague or physically inconsistent.
criteria.5-6: Uses a plausible assumed size/mass or surface gravity, with limited discussion of extreme density constraints.
criteria.7-8: Clearly parameterizes the scenario and notes feasibility limits such as exotic density or collapse risk.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames multiple viable regimes, including black-hole/Schwarzschild or material-strength limits where relevant.

criteria.name: Gravity, Tides, and Local Surface Mechanics
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates explanation of how gravity behaves on a very small massive body, including steep gradients, walking, falling, horizon effects, and orientation changes.
criteria.1-2: Gives generic high-gravity claims with little connection to tiny radius effects.
criteria.3-4: Mentions strong gravity but misses gradients, curvature, or local motion consequences.
criteria.5-6: Explains surface gravity and some effects of small radius, such as rapid horizon curvature.
criteria.7-8: Covers gravity gradients, tidal forces across the body, changing down-direction, and difficult surface movement.
criteria.9-10: Integrates surface gravity, curvature, tidal variation, and body-scale mechanics into a coherent lived experience.

criteria.name: Escape Velocity, Orbits, and Motion Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons that a tiny body can have high surface gravity yet relatively low escape velocity, producing unusual jumping, throwing, and orbital effects.
criteria.1-2: Assumes high gravity always means impossible escape or ignores escape/orbital mechanics.
criteria.3-4: Mentions jumping or escape but confuses gravity, mass, radius, and velocity relationships.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that escape speed depends on radius as well as gravity and gives plausible consequences.
criteria.7-8: Explains low escape velocity, close orbits, short orbital paths, and hazards from jumping or thrown objects.
criteria.9-10: Quantitatively or semi-quantitatively connects radius, surface gravity, escape speed, orbital period, and practical motion outcomes.

criteria.name: Habitability and Downstream Survival Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of major consequences for a human living there, including atmosphere retention, pressure, radiation, landing, structural stability, and biological stress.
criteria.1-2: Focuses on spectacle while ignoring whether a human could survive.
criteria.3-4: Mentions survival problems but only in a generic or disconnected way.
criteria.5-6: Covers several relevant issues such as atmosphere loss, extreme gravity gradients, or landing hazards.
criteria.7-8: Connects physical mechanics to breathing, movement, shelter, transport, and environmental protection.
criteria.9-10: Provides a broad, causally linked survival analysis including atmosphere, tides, engineering constraints, radiation/thermal exposure, and logistics.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence and Uncertainty Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a consistent chain from the counterfactual premise through near-term and long-term effects while clearly marking assumptions and uncertainty.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions or unsupported leaps that break the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct ideas but mixes incompatible assumptions or overstates conclusions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with assumptions stated in broad terms and only minor inconsistencies.
criteria.7-8: Builds a clear causal chain and distinguishes likely effects from parameter-dependent ones.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous consistency across all consequences, explicitly calibrating uncertainty and alternative outcomes by asteroid size, mass, and density.

items.model_answer:
If you lived on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid, your experience would depend entirely on its **density and size**, not just how “big” it looks. Gravity at the surface depends on mass and radius together. A very small object that’s extremely massive would produce surprisingly strong gravity—possibly even crushing gravity.

If the asteroid were only a few kilometers wide but packed with enormous mass (for example, made of ultra-dense material like neutron-star matter), several dramatic things would happen:

First, **surface gravity could be extreme**. Gravity increases as mass increases and decreases with radius. If the asteroid were small but incredibly dense, gravity at its surface could be far stronger than Earth’s. You might weigh many times more than you do here. Standing up could be impossible. Your bones and organs might not withstand the pressure.

Second, the **shape would likely be perfectly spherical**. Normal asteroids are lumpy because their gravity is weak. But once gravity becomes strong enough, it pulls material into a sphere. A tiny but ultra-massive object would look more like a miniature planet than a jagged rock.

Third, **escape would be difficult or impossible**. Escape velocity would be extremely high. On Earth it’s about 11 km/s. On a compact, ultra-massive asteroid, it could be much higher. If it were dense enough, it could even approach relativistic escape speeds. If it were dense beyond a certain limit, it wouldn’t be an asteroid at all—it would collapse into a black hole.

Fourth, **tidal forces could become dangerous**. If the object were small but very massive, gravity would change noticeably over short distances. Your feet could feel much stronger gravity than your head. On sufficiently compact objects, this difference could stretch you—similar to what happens near black holes, though much weaker unless the density were extreme.

Finally, **geology and environment would be strange**. The immense pressure would compress materials into exotic states. Normal rock might not even remain in its familiar form. If the object were massive enough, its interior temperature from gravitational compression could be extremely high.

In short, living on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid would likely be impossible. If it were dense enough to produce very strong gravity, it would either crush you, heat itself intensely, or collapse into something more extreme like a neutron-star fragment or black hole. A “small but super-heavy” world stops behaving like an ordinary asteroid and starts behaving like one of the most extreme objects in the universe.

items.model_answer:
In principle, yes — but not in any practical sense.

When you stir water, you’re doing mechanical work on it. Because of viscosity (internal friction between layers of water), some of that mechanical energy is converted into thermal energy. So stirring does very slightly heat the water.

However, the effect is extremely small.

To boil water, you must raise its temperature to 100 °C (at standard pressure). Heating 1 kilogram of water from room temperature (say 20 °C) to boiling requires about 334,000 joules of energy. That’s a huge amount of energy to supply just by stirring.

When you stir vigorously by hand, you might produce on the order of 10–100 watts of mechanical power. Even if every bit of that energy went into heating the water (which it doesn’t), it would take close to an hour of continuous, intense stirring to bring a single liter to a boil — and in reality, heat would continuously escape to the surroundings, making it effectively impossible.

Industrial systems can heat fluids by mechanical agitation — for example, high-speed mixers or ultrasonic devices can significantly heat liquids. But that requires powerful machinery and substantial energy input, not a spoon in a pot.

So yes, in principle stirring can heat water enough to boil it — but in practice, you would never be able to boil water just by stirring it by hand.

items.model_answer:
Neutrinos are produced in enormous numbers during a core‑collapse supernova, but they interact extraordinarily weakly with matter. About 10^58 neutrinos are released in a few seconds, and even at a distance of 10 light‑years the Earth would be flooded by roughly 10^11 neutrinos per square centimeter—yet almost all would pass straight through the planet without interacting. In fact, during Supernova 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a burst of neutrinos passed through Earth and only a couple dozen were detected in massive underground detectors; no biological effects occurred.

For neutrino radiation to become lethal, the supernova would have to be unimaginably close—so close that the neutrino flux would deposit a biologically dangerous radiation dose (on the order of several grays) in human tissue. Because neutrino interaction cross-sections are so tiny, achieving such a dose would likely require the star to explode within a few astronomical units of Earth—closer than the orbit of Jupiter, and probably closer than Earth’s orbit itself. At that distance, the star would already be part of our solar system, which is not astrophysically realistic for a massive star about to go supernova.

If a supernova did occur that close, the neutrinos would not be the main problem. The intense burst of gamma rays, X-rays, and the subsequent shock wave and ejected stellar material would devastate Earth first. The planet’s atmosphere would be stripped or severely altered, surface temperatures would spike, and the biosphere would likely be sterilized. Long-term cosmic ray bombardment would further damage the atmosphere and deplete the ozone layer.

In short, neutrinos from any realistically nearby supernova (within tens or even a few light-years) would be essentially harmless to life on Earth. Only an absurdly close supernova—so close that other effects would already destroy the planet—could make neutrino radiation lethal.

items.model_answer:
A one‑month‑old baby grows at an extraordinarily fast rate compared to later in life. In the first month, a baby might gain about 3–5 cm in length and around 1 kilogram in weight. Relative to their starting size, that’s an enormous growth rate—on the order of several percent increase in body mass per week. Human growth normally slows dramatically after infancy. But if that early rapid growth rate continued unchanged throughout life, the consequences would be extreme.

If growth stayed proportional (that is, the body kept increasing by the same percentage over time), human size would increase exponentially. Within just a few years, a child would become far larger than any current human. By adolescence, a person could be many meters tall and weigh several tons. Continuing into adulthood, their mass would reach tens or hundreds of tons, depending on the exact rate assumed.

However, biology and physics would quickly become limiting factors. The square–cube law is crucial here: as a body grows larger, its volume (and therefore weight) increases faster than the cross-sectional area of its bones and muscles. If a human scaled up proportionally, their bones would not be strong enough to support their weight. Even at a few times normal adult size, bones would fracture under the stress. The heart would struggle to pump blood high enough against gravity, leading to circulatory failure. Heat dissipation would also become a major problem, since larger bodies retain heat more easily.

Metabolic demands would be enormous. A person weighing tens of tons would require an immense caloric intake, comparable to large whales. Supplying enough oxygen would also become difficult, as lungs do not scale efficiently for very large terrestrial animals.

In reality, humans (and all animals) slow their growth precisely because of these physical and biological constraints. If we somehow ignored those limits and growth continued at a one‑month‑old’s rate, humans would rapidly reach impossible sizes, structurally collapse under their own weight, and likely die long before reaching extreme dimensions.

items.model_answer:
If a Tyrannosaurus rex were suddenly released in modern New York City, the outcome would depend on how we imagine the animal’s behavior, but several likely consequences can be reasoned from biology, physics, and urban infrastructure.

A real T. rex was about 12 meters long, weighed around 7–9 tons, and could likely run at speeds between 20 and perhaps 30 km/h for short bursts. It would be enormously strong, capable of crushing bone with a bite force far beyond any modern land predator. However, it would still be an animal, not an indestructible movie monster.

In a dense area like Manhattan, the initial impact would be chaos. People would panic, leading to stampedes, traffic accidents, and mass attempts to flee. The T. rex would probably attack moving targets out of instinct, potentially causing fatalities before authorities understood what was happening. Vehicles would not reliably stop it; a car would be like a large obstacle, but a direct collision at speed could injure the animal. Buildings, however, especially steel-and-concrete skyscrapers, would not be easily damaged. A T. rex could break windows, damage storefronts, overturn small vehicles, and possibly knock down light structures, but it could not topple modern high-rises.

Law enforcement would initially respond with small arms, which would likely be insufficient to quickly stop such a massive animal unless shots struck the brain or spine. Within a short time, heavily armed units—SWAT, National Guard, possibly even military forces—would be deployed. Large-caliber weapons, armor-piercing rounds, or anti-materiel rifles would be capable of penetrating the skull or vital organs. Given modern firepower, the animal would almost certainly be killed within hours, possibly much sooner, once authorities coordinated a response.

Environmental factors would also stress the T. rex. It evolved in a warm Cretaceous climate with high oxygen levels and different atmospheric composition. Modern air and temperatures might not be ideal. The city environment—noise, confined streets, unfamiliar surfaces like asphalt and concrete—could disorient or stress it. It might injure itself slipping or colliding with structures.

Casualties could range from dozens to potentially hundreds in a worst-case, densely packed scenario before containment, mostly from panic and initial attacks rather than prolonged predation. Economically, the damage could reach hundreds of millions or more, depending on the location and duration of the incident.

In short, a T. rex in New York City would cause brief but intense destruction and loss of life, followed by a rapid, overwhelming human military response that would end the event. The dinosaur would be terrifying, but it would not overrun or permanently threaten a modern city.

items.model_answer:
If you dumped all the world’s tea into the Great Lakes, you would not turn them into “tea” in any meaningful sense. The lakes would remain overwhelmingly water, with only a faint chemical trace of tea compounds.

Here’s why.

Global tea production is roughly 6 million metric tons per year (about 6 × 10⁹ kg of dry tea). Even if you imagined dumping an entire year’s global production into the lakes at once, that amount is tiny compared to the volume of the Great Lakes.

The Great Lakes contain about 22,700 cubic kilometers of water. Since 1 cubic kilometer of water has a mass of about 10¹² kilograms, the lakes together contain roughly 2.3 × 10¹⁶ kilograms of water.

Now compare the two:

Tea: ~6 × 10⁹ kg  
Water: ~2.3 × 10¹⁶ kg  

That’s a ratio of about 1 part tea to 4 million parts water.

Even if every bit of the tea fully dissolved (which it wouldn’t — most of it is leaf material that doesn’t dissolve), the resulting concentration would be extremely weak. For comparison, a normal cup of tea uses about 2 grams of tea in 250 grams of water — a ratio of about 1 to 125. The Great Lakes mixture would be about 30,000 times more dilute than a normal cup of tea.

Visually, you probably wouldn’t notice much change. The lakes already contain dissolved organic matter from plants and soil that gives some areas a brownish tint. Adding all the world’s annual tea production might slightly increase organic content locally at first, but once dispersed, the color change would be negligible.

Ecologically, however, there would be effects. The added organic matter would decompose. Microbes would break it down, consuming oxygen in the process. If dumped all at once in a confined area, it could temporarily cause oxygen depletion (a local dead zone) and harm fish. But spread across all five lakes, the impact would likely be modest relative to their vast size and natural organic inputs.

In short: dumping all the world’s tea into the Great Lakes would not create a giant cup of tea. It would produce an extremely dilute organic addition — environmentally noticeable in some areas, perhaps disruptive if concentrated, but physically insignificant compared to the immense scale of the lakes.
